rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).

criteria.criterion: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)

rows.question: Does the obligation to indicate that deep-fakes are artificially generated apply when prosecuting a criminal offence?
rows.answer: No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

criteria.criterion: No
Deep-fake disclosure exemption covers detection, prevention, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences

rows.question: When the intended use of an AI system is listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act, the AI system is automatically high-risk, isn't it? If not, can you explain when that is not the case?
rows.answer: Not always. Under Article 6(2) an AI system falling within one of the lettered use cases listed under the eight areas of Annex III is high-risk, but Article 6(3) provides a derogation: such a system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and it is intended to perform a narrow procedural task, to improve the result of a previously completed human activity, to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. That derogation never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk. A provider relying on Article 6(3) must document that assessment before placing the system on the market and still register the system in the EU database under Article 49.

criteria.criterion: No
Exception applies where system does not pose significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing outcome of decision making

Exception requires one of: narrow procedural task; improving result of previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing/influencing human assessment; preparatory task to an Annex III assessment
Exception never applies (system is always high-risk) if it performs profiling of natural persons

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No, the AI system is high-risk, because the Act recognises no "medium risk" tier and does not import the sectoral risk class of the host product. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where both conditions are met: it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes the Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for its placing on the market. Both limbs are satisfied here, so the medical device's own "medium-risk" classification is irrelevant to the AI classification. The consequence is that the Chapter III Section 2 requirements apply to the AI system and, under Article 43(3), they are assessed as part of the MDR notified-body conformity assessment procedure, a single integrated procedure covering both regimes.

criteria.criterion: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification

rows.question: Does the EU AI Act explicitly requires to use explainable AI techniques such as LIME or SHAP to increase the trustworthiness of high-risk AI systems?
rows.answer: No, the EU AI Act mandates no specific explainable-AI technique such as LIME or SHAP, and Article 13 instead requires only that high-risk AI systems be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret their output. Article 14 requires effective human oversight, and Article 15 requires appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.

criteria.criterion: No
Article 13 requires sufficient transparency/interpretability for deployers, without naming a technique
Requirement is outcome-based and technology-neutral, leaving choice of method to the provider

rows.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to AI systems or AI models or both?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk.

criteria.criterion: Both AI systems and AI models
Art 2(1)(a): providers placing/putting into service AI systems
Art 2(1)(a): providers placing general-purpose AI models on the market

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: Not prohibited, and not high-risk on the biometrics route. Biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be is expressly excluded from the remote biometric identification use case in Annex III(1)(a), so Article 6(2) does not classify it as high-risk on that basis, and it is none of the practices banned by Article 5, which reaches biometric categorisation only where the system deduces or infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. It would nonetheless become high-risk if the verification function serves another listed Annex III use case, for example verifying candidates in recruitment or worker management under Annex III(4), or if under Article 6(1) it is a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment. Absent those conditions the system is limited risk at most, since Article 50 imposes transparency duties only on the specified interaction, synthetic-content, emotion recognition and biometric categorisation scenarios, none of which a pure identity-confirmation check engages.

criteria.criterion: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion

rows.question: Are AI safety components within medical devices of MDR class IIa, IIb, or III considered to be high-risk according to the EU AI Act? Why?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a medical device is high-risk under Article 6(1), because both cumulative conditions are met: the product is covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR) at point 11, and a device of MDR class IIa, IIb or III must undergo a third-party conformity assessment involving a notified body before being placed on the market or put into service. Class I devices, which self-certify without notified-body involvement, do not satisfy the Article 6(1)(b) condition and are therefore not high-risk on this route. The applicable conformity assessment for such a safety component is governed by Article 43, carried out within the notified-body procedure under the MDR itself, so the Chapter III Section 2 requirements are verified through the sectoral assessment rather than a separate parallel procedure.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Condition: AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (the MDR)
Condition: that product must undergo third-party (notified body) conformity assessment to be placed on the market (Article 6(1))
MDR classes IIa, IIb, III require notified-body conformity assessment, so both cumulative conditions are met

rows.question: What documentation does a provider of a high-risk AI system needs to keep available for the national competent authorities, and for how long?
rows.answer: Under Article 18, for ten years after the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, the provider must keep at the disposal of the national competent authorities the technical documentation (Article 11), the quality-management-system documentation (Article 17), the documentation of any changes approved by notified bodies, the decisions and other documents issued by notified bodies, and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47). Separately, under Article 19 the automatically generated logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months.

criteria.criterion: Technical documentation (Article 11)
Quality management system documentation (Article 17)
Notified body change documentation and decisions/other documents, where applicable
EU declaration of conformity (Article 47)
10 years after the system is placed on the market or put into service

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Article 14 governs human oversight, requiring high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use. The measures under Article 14(4) must enable those persons to understand the system's capabilities and limitations and monitor its operation, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret the output, decide not to use the system or disregard, override or reverse the output, and intervene or interrupt operation through a stop button or similar procedure.

criteria.criterion: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system

rows.question: What is the meaning and purpose of 'testing data' in the context of AI systems, and why is it important that it is not leaked during the training process?
rows.answer: Testing data is defined in Article 3(32) as data used to provide an independent evaluation of the AI system, in order to confirm its expected performance before it is placed on the market or put into service. If testing data leaks into the training process, the system is in effect assessed on data it has already seen, which inflates its apparent performance and defeats the purpose of the independent check that Article 10 requires for the datasets of a high-risk AI system.

criteria.criterion: Testing data is one of the training/validation/testing data sets under Article 10(1), used to check the high-risk AI system against its intended purpose after training and validation

It must meet the Article 10(3) quality criteria: relevant, sufficiently representative, to the best extent possible free of errors, complete, and with appropriate statistical properties for the intended purpose

Leakage of training data into the testing set destroys the set's independence, so it can no longer reliably verify Article 10(3) compliance and instead yields inflated, misleading accuracy that masks errors, biases or gaps

rows.question: What are the high-risk uses of AI systems listed under 'Administration of justice and democratic processes' cited in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Annex III point 8 lists two high-risk use cases under administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex III point 8(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority, or on its behalf, to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used similarly in alternative dispute resolution. Annex III point 8(b) covers AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, with a carve-out for tools that only organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

criteria.criterion: AI systems assisting a judicial authority (or on its behalf) in researching/interpreting facts and law and applying law to facts, or used similarly in alternative dispute resolution
AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote
Exclusion: does not cover AI systems whose output natural persons are not directly exposed to, e.g. tools organising/optimising/structuring political campaigns administratively or logistically

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.

criteria.criterion: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk

rows.question: Which AI systems used in education or vocational training should be classified as high-risk according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Four use cases under the education and vocational training area of Annex III are high-risk, and they are classified as such by Article 6(2), which makes any AI system listed in Annex III high-risk. They are systems intended to determine access or admission or to assign natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels, systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes, including where those outcomes are used to steer the learning process, systems intended to assess the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or be able to access, and systems intended for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests. Each applies in the context of or within educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. Under the Article 6(3) derogation such a system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, but it remains high-risk whenever it profiles natural persons, and the provider must document that self-assessment before placing the system on the market.

criteria.criterion: Access, admission, or assignment to educational/vocational training institutions at all levels
Evaluating learning outcomes, including to steer the learning process
Assessing the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or can access
Monitoring/detecting prohibited student behaviour during tests

rows.question: What obligations, if any, does the EU AI Act set in place for AI systems that interact directly with natural persons? What exceptions, if any, apply?
rows.answer: Providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the persons concerned are informed they are interacting with an AI system, under the transparency obligation in Article 50(1), unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and context of use. That information must be given to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements under Article 50(5). One exception applies: the disclosure duty does not attach to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties. That exception is itself reversed where such systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence, in which case the Article 50(1) disclosure is required.

criteria.criterion: Obligation: providers must design/develop the system so natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system
Exception: not required where obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, given the circumstances and context of use

Exception: AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to safeguards for third parties' rights and freedoms — unless available for the public to report a criminal offence

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibition of AI practices attracts administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, where the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, under Article 99(3). This is the highest of the three ceilings in the penalty regime, above the EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % tier in Article 99(4) for operator and notified-body breaches and the EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % tier in Article 99(5) for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or competent authorities. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) reverses the rule so the applicable ceiling is the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount. Article 5 is the provision breached, prohibiting eight practices including subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement.

criteria.criterion: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices

rows.question: How does Annex II relate to prohibited uses of AI systems?
rows.answer: Annex II does not itself prohibit anything. It operates as the closed list of serious criminal offences referred to in Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h)(iii), which is one of the three narrow exceptions to the Article 5 prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, and the offence must be punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence of at least four years. The listed offences are terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives, murder, grievous bodily injury, illicit trade in human organs or tissue, illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials, kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking, crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships, rape, environmental crime, organised or armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of those offences. Outside those exhaustively listed offences and the other two objectives in Article 5, namely the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and for missing persons, and the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety or a genuine and foreseeable terrorist attack, the practice remains a prohibited practice. Annex II therefore has no bearing on the other prohibitions in Article 5, such as social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images, or emotion recognition in workplaces and education institutions.

criteria.criterion: Annex II lists criminal offences (does not itself prohibit anything)
Referenced in Article 5(1)(h)(iii) as basis for one exception to the Article 5(1)(h) prohibition on 'real-time' remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement
Exception (localising/identifying a suspect) applies only if the offence is listed in Annex II and punishable by a custodial sentence/detention order of max at least four years

rows.question: Can the European Commission amend Annex III of the EU AI Act to add or modify use-cases classified as high-risk AI systems? Under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes, the Commission may amend Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases of high-risk AI systems through delegated acts adopted in accordance with Article 97, under Article 7(1). Both conditions must be fulfilled cumulatively: the AI systems are intended to be used in one of the areas already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk posed by the high-risk AI systems already referred to in Annex III. When assessing that second condition the Commission must weigh the Article 7(2) criteria, including the intended purpose, the extent of use, the nature and amount of data processed, the degree of autonomy, the severity and reversibility of harm, and the availability of redress. The Commission cannot create a new area, only add or modify use-cases within the existing areas, and Article 7(3) separately allows removal of a use-case where it no longer poses significant risks to fundamental rights, health or safety and the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection under Union law. Procedurally, Article 97 confers the power for five years from 1 August 2024 with tacit extension, requires consultation of experts designated by each Member State before adoption, and the act enters into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within three months of notification, extendable by a further three months.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Condition: AI intended to be used in any of the areas listed in Annex III
Condition: posed risk is equal or greater than those already referred to in Annex III
Both conditions must apply ("and" clause)

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful.

criteria.criterion: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person

rows.question: Should market surveilance authorities be provided with remote access to documentations and data sets used to develop a high-risk AI system?
rows.answer: Yes, where relevant and limited to what is necessary for their tasks. Article 74(12) requires providers to grant market surveillance authorities full access to the documentation as well as the training, validation and testing data sets used for the development of high-risk AI systems, including, where appropriate and subject to security safeguards, through application programming interfaces or other relevant technical means and tools enabling remote access. This access power operates without prejudice to the powers under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, which frames the authorities' investigation and corrective-measure powers. Source code is a narrower matter under Article 74(13): it is granted only upon a reasoned request, and only where it is necessary to assess conformity with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements and where testing, auditing and verification based on the data and documentation provided have been exhausted or proved insufficient.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Full access to documentation and to training, validation and testing data sets, granted by providers, limited to what is necessary for the authority's tasks
Remote access (e.g. via API or other technical means) permitted only "where appropriate" and subject to security safeguards

rows.question: If a provider of a high-risk AI system confirms that the system achieves an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity at the time of development, then no further action is required by the provider on these aspects in the future. Correct?
rows.answer: No. Article 15(1) requires high-risk AI systems to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and to perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle, so a single confirmation at the development stage does not discharge the obligation. Article 9(1) requires the risk management system to be established, implemented, documented and maintained as a continuous, iterative process across the whole lifecycle, including evaluation of data gathered from post-market monitoring, and Article 9(5) requires testing to ensure the system performs consistently for its intended purpose. The quality management system under Article 17 must include examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development, together with the frequency at which they are performed, and procedures for the management of modifications to the system. The accuracy levels and relevant accuracy metrics declared in the accompanying instructions of use under Article 15 must accordingly remain accurate as to the performance that can be expected.

criteria.criterion: No
Must perform consistently throughout lifecycle, including resilience to errors/faults/inconsistencies (Art. 15(1),(4))
Cybersecurity resilience against third-party exploitation is ongoing, not one-time (Art. 15(5))
Accuracy levels/metrics must be declared in instructions of use (Art. 15(3))

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems have no mandatory duties under the Act, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

criteria.criterion: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)

rows.question: Does "systemic risk" apply to AI systems or general purpose AI models or both?
rows.answer: Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.

criteria.criterion: Applies to general-purpose AI models only (Article 51), not to AI systems
Systemic risk classification applies only to general-purpose AI models (Article 51), not to AI systems

rows.question: Are AI systems that fall under one of the areas of Annex III, but not falling within a use-case within such areas, considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Article 6(2) classifies a system as high-risk only where it falls within one of the use-cases specifically listed under the eight areas of Annex III, so a numbered area heading such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, or administration of justice and democratic processes is not itself an operative trigger. A system merely operating in such a sector, without matching a lettered use-case entry, is not high-risk on the Annex III route. It may still be high-risk on the separate Annex I route under Article 6(1), where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment.

criteria.criterion: No
High-risk requires falling within a specific enumerated use case listed in Annex III, not merely within the broader area grouping those use cases
Annex III areas are organisational headings; the operative trigger is the individual use-case description

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

criteria.criterion: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))

rows.question: If I have an AI system that is high-risk because listed in the use cases of Annex III, and change it to a different use case that is not in Annex I or III, does it stay high-risk due to its historical provenance?
rows.answer: No, high-risk status does not attach as a matter of historical provenance. Classification under Article 6 is assessed against the system's intended purpose at the relevant time, so a system is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I that must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation (Article 6(1)), or where it falls within one of the lettered use cases under the eight areas of Annex III (Article 6(2)). Once the intended purpose is genuinely changed to a use case listed in neither Annex I nor Annex III, and the system is no longer intended for the former Annex III use case, it is not high-risk going forward. The reclassification must be reflected in the intended purpose as declared and in the instructions for use, and it does not retroactively cure any non-compliance during the period the system was placed on the market or put into service for the Annex III use case.

criteria.criterion: No
High-risk status under Article 6 depends on the AI system's current intended purpose/use case, not its prior classification
If the new use case falls outside both Annex I and Annex III, neither condition in Article 6(1) or 6(2) is met, so the system is not high-risk

rows.question: How are AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum classified, and what exception is given for certain campaign-related tools?
rows.answer: Under Annex III point 8(b), AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, are high-risk under Article 6(2). Annex III point 8(b) itself excludes systems to whose output natural persons are not directly exposed, such as tools used only to organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view, which therefore fall outside this high-risk category.

criteria.criterion: High-risk classification under Annex III, point 8(b)
Covers AI systems influencing election/referendum outcome or voters' voting behaviour
Exception: AI systems whose output natural persons are not directly exposed to are excluded
Example given: tools organising/optimising/structuring political campaigns administratively or logistically

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Article 1(1) states that the purpose of the Regulation is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation. To that end, Article 1(2) lays down harmonised rules for the placing on the market, putting into service and use of AI systems, prohibitions of certain AI practices, specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for their operators, harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems, harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models, rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement, and measures to support innovation with a particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups.

criteria.criterion: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which specific AI systems are explicitly listed as high-risk because they make decisions in critical life- and health-related situations involving emergency calls and triage?
rows.answer: Under Annex III point 5(d), AI systems intended to be used for dispatching or prioritising in dispatching emergency first-response services, or for triage of emergency medical-service patients (including by fire brigades and medical aid), are explicitly listed as high-risk. They fall within the 'essential private and public services' category of the eight Annex III high-risk use cases and are classified as high-risk through the Annex III route of Article 6(2), which treats any system falling within a listed use case as high-risk.

criteria.criterion: AI systems that evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons
AI systems used to dispatch, or establish priority in dispatching, emergency first response services (police, firefighters, medical aid)
Emergency healthcare patient triage systems

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as part of their supervisory role for an AI regulatory sandbox, compliance with which specific Article must the market surveillance authority verify?
rows.answer: Article 60, which governs testing of high-risk AI systems in real world conditions and sets the conditions for it, including an approved real-world testing plan submitted to the market surveillance authority, informed consent of test subjects, and registration in the EU database. Article 76(2) makes this explicit: where testing in real world conditions is conducted for AI systems supervised within an AI regulatory sandbox, the market surveillance authorities verify compliance with Article 60 as part of their supervisory role for that sandbox. Those authorities may, as appropriate, allow the provider or prospective provider to conduct the testing in derogation from the conditions in Article 60(4), points (f) and (g).

criteria.criterion: Article 60

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions: it performs a narrow procedural task, it improves the result of a previously completed human activity, it detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or it performs a preparatory task. Under Article 6(3), this exception never applies where the system profiles natural persons. The provider must document the assessment before placing the system on the market and register it under Article 49(2).

criteria.criterion: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))

rows.question: Is an AI system used to detect decision-making patterns or deviations for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: Even within an Annex III use case, Article 6(3)(c) provides that an AI system intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm and is not meant to replace or influence a previously completed human assessment without proper human review. However, under Article 6(3) such a system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons.

criteria.criterion: No, not by default
Condition: not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review
Exception: always high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons

rows.question: Regarding the European Artificial Intelligence Board: (1) Who designates its members? (2) How long is the term? How many times is the term renewable? (3) must members represent stakeholder interests or act impartially/objectively? (4) what voting threshold is required to adopt the Board's rules of procedure (is a simple 50%+1 majority enough)?
rows.answer: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (Article 65) has one representative per Member State, each serving a three-year term renewable once under Article 65(3). Under Article 65(4) each is their Member State's single contact point rather than an independent stakeholder appointee, while Article 65(7) requires the Board to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities. Its rules of procedure are adopted by a two-thirds majority under Article 65(5), so a simple majority is not sufficient.

criteria.criterion: Members designated by their Member State
Term is three years, renewable once
No stakeholder representation requirement; must safeguard objectivity/impartiality
Two-thirds majority required to adopt rules of procedure (simple majority not enough)

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Unlimited jurisdiction to review. Article 101(5) confers on the Court of Justice of the European Union unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine on a provider of a general-purpose AI model under that Article, and it may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed. Those fines are the Commission's own enforcement measure against general-purpose AI model providers of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for infringements of the Chapter V obligations, for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, or for failure to comply with a requested measure. Before adopting such a decision the Commission must communicate its preliminary findings to the provider and give it an opportunity to be heard under Article 101(2), and the fine must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive under Article 101(3).

criteria.criterion: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine

rows.question: Consider the situation in which a market surveillance authority (MSA) determines that an AI system, originally classified as non-high-risk by the provider, is in fact high-risk. Does the provider need to recall and suspend the use of the system without undue delay, or does the MSA provide a timeframe within which the provider can take corrective actions? Or does this depend on the gravity of the situation?
rows.answer: The market surveillance authority prescribes the timeframe, and immediate recall is not automatically required. Under Article 80(2), where the authority's evaluation finds that a system the provider classified as non-high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation is in fact high-risk, it must without undue delay require that provider to take all necessary actions to bring the system into compliance with this Regulation and to take appropriate corrective action within a period the authority may prescribe. The gravity of the situation does matter, because where the system also presents a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, Article 79(2) requires the authority to order corrective action, withdrawal from the market or recall within a period it may prescribe, and in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period laid down in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation. Independently of any order, Article 20 obliges the provider, once it considers or has reason to consider the high-risk AI system non-conforming, to immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring it into conformity, withdraw it, disable it or recall it, and to inform the distributors, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers accordingly.

criteria.criterion: MSA sets a compliance/corrective-action period for the provider, rather than an automatic without-undue-delay recall/suspension duty
Provider must bring the system into compliance and take corrective action within that MSA-prescribed period (Article 80(2) and 80(4))
Failure to comply within that period triggers fines under Article 99 (and Article 79(5)-(9) applies), not gravity-based variation of the timeframe

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what presumption applies when a high-risk AI system is trained and tested on data that reflects the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used?
rows.answer: Such a system is presumed to comply with the relevant requirements of Article 10(4), which requires data sets to take into account the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting in which the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. This presumption of conformity arises under Article 42(1) and extends only to that data governance requirement, not to the remainder of Article 10.

criteria.criterion: Presumed compliant with Article 10(3) representativeness/quality requirement for that setting
Presumption is limited to the extent required by the intended purpose
Not an exemption from other Article 10 obligations (e.g., bias examination/mitigation)

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: The provider, or where applicable the authorised representative, must register itself and the system and enter the Annex VIII Section A data into the EU database that the Commission sets up and maintains under Article 71, and must do so under Article 49(1) before the high-risk AI system listed in Annex III is placed on the market or put into service. The required items are the name, address and contact details of the provider, the same details of any person submitting the information on the provider's behalf, the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative where applicable, the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability of the AI system, a description of the intended purpose of the system and of the components and functions supported through it, a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic, the status of the AI system (on the market, in service, no longer placed on the market or in service, recalled), the certificate issued by the notified body together with a scanned copy of that certificate where applicable, electronic instructions for use, and, optionally, a URL for additional information. Electronic instructions for use are not provided for high-risk AI systems in the areas of law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management referred to in Annex III points 1, 6 and 7. Systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III fall outside this registration and are registered at national level under Article 49(5), while a provider that has concluded under Article 6(3) that its Annex III system is not high-risk must still register itself and that system under Article 49(2).

criteria.criterion: Registration confined to secure, non-public section of EU database (Article 71)
Annex VIII Section A points 1-10, excluding 6, 8 and 9
Annex VIII Section B points 1-5, 8 and 9
Annex VIII Section C points 1-3
Annex IX points 1, 2, 3 and 5

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what is an "AI regulatory sandbox"? Provide the definition elements (what it is, who sets it up, for whom it is intended, to do what, for how long).
rows.answer: A controlled framework set up by a competent authority which offers providers or prospective providers of AI systems the possibility to develop, train, validate and test, where appropriate in real-world conditions, an innovative AI system, pursuant to a sandbox plan for a limited time under regulatory supervision.

criteria.criterion: Controlled environment established by a national competent authority (or jointly with other Member States, or by the EDPS for Union bodies)
Intended for providers or prospective providers of AI systems
Purpose: fosters innovation and facilitates development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems (may include supervised real-world testing)
Time-limited, prior to market placement/putting into service, pursuant to a specific sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what transparency obligation applies to deployers when they use an AI system to generate or manipulate text for the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest, and what are the two exceptions where this obligation does not apply?
rows.answer: Under Article 50(4), a deployer that uses an AI system to generate or manipulate text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated. Under Article 50(4), that disclosure duty does not apply in two cases: first, where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; and second, where the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication of the content.

criteria.criterion: Deployers must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated
Exception 1: use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences
Exception 2: AI-generated content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system.

criteria.criterion: Language: drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established
Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is there a simplified way for SMEs (including startups) to provide the technical documentation for high-risk AI systems, and who must accept it for conformity assessment?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11(1), SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the technical documentation elements set out in Annex IV in a simplified manner, using a simplified form the Commission is required to establish for the needs of small and micro enterprises. Where an SME opts to use that form, the notified body performing the conformity assessment must accept it.

criteria.criterion: Yes
AI Office develops a simplified technical documentation form for SMEs/microenterprises, including start-ups, covering the Annex IV elements
The notified body assessing conformity of the high-risk AI system must accept that simplified form

rows.question:
Under the EU AI Act, must an employer inform affected workers and workers' representatives before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system in the workplace?
If so, should possibly specific rules or procedures be followed to provide this information?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 26(7), a deployer that is an employer must, before putting a high-risk AI system into service or using it at the workplace, inform the workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of that high-risk AI system. Under Article 26(7), that information must be provided, where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on the information of workers and their representatives.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Timing: before putting into service or using the system at the workplace
Recipients: workers' representatives and affected workers
Procedure: follow applicable Union/national law and practice on informing workers, where applicable (no separate free-standing procedure)

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict, documented access controls to prevent misuse (c); no transmission or transfer to other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).

criteria.criterion: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what specific information must a provider/prospective provider submit (and keep up to date) regarding testing of a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside an AI regulatory sandbox?
rows.answer: The provider or prospective provider must draw up a real world testing plan and submit it to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the testing is to be conducted, and the testing may proceed only in accordance with that approved plan under Article 60. Article 60 further requires the testing in real world conditions, and the provider or prospective provider conducting it, to be registered in the dedicated section of the EU database, which yields a Union-wide unique single identification number and the information accompanying that registration. That registered information must be kept up to date for the duration of the testing, including any suspension or termination and the outcome of the testing. Article 60 also conditions the testing on the informed consent of the test subjects and on supervision by the market surveillance authority, and the Commission specifies the detailed elements of the real world testing plan by implementing acts.

criteria.criterion: Real-world testing plan submitted to (and approved by) the market surveillance authority of the Member State of testing
Registration of the testing with a Union-wide unique single identification number
General rule: registration under Article 71(4) with information specified in Annex IX

Exceptions: Annex III points 1, 6, 7 (law enforcement/migration/asylum/border control) register in secure non-public EU database section per Article 49(4)(d); Annex III point 2 systems register per Article 49(5)

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, if a deployer has reason to believe that the use of a high-risk AI system may present a risk, what must the deployer do, and whom must the deployer inform?
rows.answer: The deployer must, without undue delay, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and must suspend the use of that system, under Article 26(5), which applies where the deployer has reason to consider that use in accordance with the instructions for use may result in the system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), namely a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights. That same paragraph requires the deployer to monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use and, where relevant, to inform the provider in accordance with Article 72 on post-market monitoring. Where the deployer has identified a serious incident, it must immediately inform first the provider, and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities. If the provider cannot be reached, Article 73 on serious incident reporting applies mutatis mutandis, and the notification duty does not extend to sensitive operational data of deployers that are law enforcement authorities.

criteria.criterion: Inform the provider or distributor
Inform the relevant market surveillance authority
Suspend use of the system
All actions taken without undue delay

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Article 13 requires a high-risk AI system to be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, and Article 13(3) prescribes the minimum content of the accompanying instructions for use. That content comprises the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance including the intended purpose, the level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, any known or foreseeable circumstance related to use in accordance with the intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse which may lead to risks to health and safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2), the system's performance as regards the persons or groups on which it is intended to be used, specifications for the input data, information enabling deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately, the changes to the system and its performance pre-determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment, the human oversight measures referred to in Article 14 including the technical measures put in place to facilitate interpretation of outputs, the computational and hardware resources needed together with the expected lifetime and the necessary maintenance and care measures including software updates, and, where relevant, a description of the mechanisms within the system allowing deployers to properly collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12. This information must be provided in a concise, complete, correct and clear form that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers.

criteria.criterion: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what actions must a provider take when it considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation?
rows.answer: The provider must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring the system into conformity, to withdraw it, to disable it, or to recall it, as appropriate, under Article 20.1. It must inform the distributors of the high-risk AI system concerned and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. Where that system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79.1 and the provider becomes aware of the risk, Article 20.2 requires it to immediately investigate the causes in collaboration with the reporting deployer, and to inform the market surveillance authorities competent for the system and, where applicable, the notified body that issued a certificate for it, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. Article 16 anchors these duties in the provider's core obligations, requiring it to take the necessary corrective actions and provide the information required by Article 20.

criteria.criterion: Immediately take necessary corrective action: bring into conformity, withdraw, disable, or recall, as appropriate
Inform distributors of the system concerned
Where applicable, inform deployers, authorised representative and importers accordingly

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, what is the definition of (a) a "conformity assessment body" and (b) "conformity assessment"?
rows.answer: A "conformity assessment body" is defined in Article 3(21) as a body that performs third-party conformity assessment activities, including testing, certification and inspection. "Conformity assessment" is defined in Article 3(20) as the process of demonstrating whether the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 relating to a high-risk AI system have been fulfilled.

criteria.criterion: Conformity assessment body: a body that performs third-party conformity assessment activities
Conformity assessment body: activities include testing, certification and inspection
Conformity assessment: the process of demonstrating whether the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements for a high-risk AI system have been fulfilled

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up under Article 95(3) by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, including with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, such as civil society organisations and academia. The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate their drawing up under Article 95(1), including the related governance mechanisms, to foster voluntary application to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems of some or all of the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2, taking account of available technical solutions and industry best practices. Under Article 95(4) the AI Office and the Member States must take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, when doing so. A single code may cover one or more AI systems, taking into account the similarity of their intended purpose.

criteria.criterion: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which AI systems in the financial services area are classified as high-risk under Annex III(5)(b), and what explicit exceptions are listed?
rows.answer: AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or to establish their credit score are high-risk under Annex III(5)(b), which sits within the Annex III area on access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits, and is classified high-risk through the Annex III use-case route in Article 6(2). The single explicit exception stated in that point is for AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud, which therefore falls outside Annex III(5)(b). Separately, insurance-related pricing is addressed in its own point, Annex III(5)(c), covering AI systems used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance.

criteria.criterion: AI systems evaluating creditworthiness or establishing credit score of natural persons
Exception: AI systems used for detecting financial fraud

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider established outside the EU do in order to place a high-risk AI system on the Union market?
rows.answer: A provider established in a third country must, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union before making its high-risk AI system available on the Union market (Article 22(1)). The provider must enable that authorised representative to perform the tasks specified in the mandate (Article 22(2)). The mandate is not merely formal: the authorised representative must terminate it, and immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority and, where applicable, the notified body, if it has reason to consider the provider to be acting contrary to its obligations under the Regulation (Article 22(4)).

criteria.criterion: Appoint an authorised representative established in the Union, by written mandate
Must occur prior to making the system available on the Union market

Representative empowered per Article 22(3) tasks (verify conformity documentation, retain records 10 years, provide information/log access to authorities, cooperate with authorities, handle registration)

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Article 17(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to put in place a quality management system that ensures compliance with the Regulation, documented in a systematic and orderly manner in written policies, procedures and instructions. Its minimum elements are a strategy for regulatory compliance including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for the management of modifications, techniques and procedures for design, design control and design verification, techniques and procedures for development, quality control and quality assurance, examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development and their frequency, technical specifications including standards to be applied, systems and procedures for data management covering acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention, the risk management system required by Article 9, the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system under Article 72, procedures for the reporting of a serious incident under Article 73, the handling of communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities, notified bodies and other operators, systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information, resource management including security-of-supply measures, and an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and other staff. Under Article 17(2) implementation of those aspects must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, while respecting in any event the degree of rigour and level of protection needed for compliance. Providers already subject to quality management obligations or an equivalent function under sectoral Union law may include these aspects in that system under Article 17(3), and under Article 17(4) financial institutions complying with internal governance arrangements or processes under Union financial services law are deemed to fulfil the obligation, with the exception of points (g), (h) and (i).

criteria.criterion: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what additional obligations apply to providers of a general-purpose AI model that is classified as a model with systemic risk?
rows.answer: Providers of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk must comply with four obligations under Article 55 in addition to the baseline Article 53 duties, namely performing model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks, assessing and mitigating possible systemic risks at Union level including their sources arising from development, placing on the market or use of the model, keeping track of, documenting and reporting without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures, and ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and for its physical infrastructure. Classification as a model with systemic risk follows Article 51, either through high-impact capabilities, presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations, or by Commission decision on the Annex XIII criteria. The Article 53 baseline continues to apply, meaning technical documentation of the model per Annex XI, information and documentation for downstream providers per Annex XII, a policy to comply with Union copyright law, and a publicly available sufficiently detailed summary of the training content, and the Article 53(2) exemption for free and open-source models from the documentation duties does not extend to models with systemic risk. Compliance may be demonstrated through the codes of practice facilitated by the AI Office under Article 56 until a harmonised standard is published.

criteria.criterion: Perform state-of-the-art model evaluation including documented adversarial testing to identify/mitigate systemic risks
Assess and mitigate possible Union-level systemic risks, including their sources
Track, document and report serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office/national competent authorities without undue delay
Ensure adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what are the four grounds on which non-compliance with the Act may be alleged (as listed in Article 79(6))?
rows.answer: Article 79.6 requires the notifying market surveillance authority to indicate whether the alleged non-compliance is due to one or more of four grounds: non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5, a failure of a high-risk AI system to meet the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, shortcomings in the harmonised standards or common specifications referred to in Articles 40 and 41 conferring a presumption of conformity, and non-compliance with Article 50. These indications accompany the notification details identifying the non-compliant AI system, its origin and supply chain, the nature of the non-compliance and risk involved, the nature and duration of the national measures taken, and the arguments put forward by the relevant operator.

criteria.criterion: Non-compliance with prohibition of AI practices under Article 5
Failure of high-risk AI system to meet Chapter III, Section 2 requirements
Shortcomings in harmonised standards/common specifications under Articles 40-41
Non-compliance with Article 50

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Three exhaustive objectives only, and each use must be strictly necessary. Article 5(1)(h) permits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes solely for the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation as well as the search for missing persons, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons or of a genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack, and the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation, prosecution or executing a criminal penalty. That third objective is confined to the offences listed in Annex II, which enumerates terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs, weapons or nuclear material, murder, kidnapping, rape, armed robbery, organised crime, participation in a criminal organisation and environmental crime, and only where the offence is punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence of at least four years. Any such deployment further requires prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation, with an urgency exception allowing use to begin before authorisation provided it is requested without undue delay and within 24 hours, failing which use must stop immediately, and the deployer must notify the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority.

criteria.criterion: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order

rows.question: Under Article 32 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, when is a conformity assessment body presumed to comply with the requirements in Article 31?
rows.answer: A conformity assessment body is presumed to comply with Article 31 where it demonstrates its conformity with the criteria laid down in the relevant harmonised standards, or parts thereof, the references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union, and that presumption extends only in so far as those applicable harmonised standards cover those requirements (Article 32). Article 31 sets the substantive requirements so presumed, including establishment under the national law of a Member State with legal personality, independence from the provider and from the AI system assessed, no involvement in the design, marketing or use of the systems assessed, safeguards against conflicts of interest, documented confidentiality procedures, sufficient permanent personnel with competences in AI technologies, data and computing, adequate cybersecurity, and appropriate liability insurance unless liability is assumed by the Member State.

criteria.criterion: Body demonstrates conformity with relevant harmonised standards (or parts thereof)
Condition: references to those standards published in the Official Journal of the European Union
Presumption limited to the extent those standards cover the Article 31 requirements

rows.question: Who is entitled to lodge a complaint about an infringement, and to which authority must the complaint be submitted?
rows.answer: Any natural or legal person having grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the Regulation may submit a complaint, and it must be submitted to the relevant market surveillance authority under Article 85. The right is not limited to infringements affecting the complainant's own rights, and it operates without prejudice to other administrative or judicial remedies. Such complaints must be taken into account for the purpose of conducting market surveillance activities and handled in line with the dedicated procedures established by the market surveillance authorities under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020.

criteria.criterion: Any natural or legal person
Grounds to consider there has been an infringement of the Regulation
Submitted to the relevant market surveillance authority

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure under Article 50(2) that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. That technical solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. The marking duty does not apply to the extent the AI system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof, nor where the system is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.
