The Article 5(1)(d) prohibition on assessing or predicting the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence does not bite either, because it targets assessments based solely on profiling or on personality traits and characteristics and expressly does not apply to systems supporting human assessment of involvement in criminal activity that is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to that activity, which is what a current-cart and checkout discrepancy is. Article 5(1)(c) social scoring is also not met, since it requires evaluation or classification of natural persons over a certain period of time based on social behaviour or inferred personal characteristics, with the resulting social score leading to detrimental or unfavourable treatment in unrelated social contexts or treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate, whereas a single transaction-level flag resolved by a bag check in the same context is neither persistent scoring nor cross-context. The classification would change if the tool were extended to accumulate customer profiles over time, to infer personal or personality characteristics, or to be operated on behalf of law enforcement authorities.

criteria.criterion: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions

rows.question: We are a private educational institution intending to deploy an AI tool that analyses students' prior grades and learning outcomes to recommend whether they should follow the standard or accelerated honours track going forward. We remark that a student who receives the "standard" recommendation is *not* barred from choosing accelerated, the system merely provides a suggestion. Are there reasons to believe the system might be high-risk? What articles/annex and specific points, if any, concern this use case?
rows.answer: Likely high-risk. The tool evaluates learning outcomes in order to steer the learning process, and it assesses the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or be able to access, which are the Annex III(3)(b) and Annex III(3)(c) use cases in the education and vocational training area, high-risk under Article 6(2); the private status of the institution is irrelevant, since Annex III(3) covers educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. The advisory framing does not remove that classification: the Article 6(3) derogation applies only where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and a track recommendation built on a student's prior grades is intended precisely to influence which learning pathway is taken. Article 6(3) is further excluded because a system assessing individuals against their own historical performance data performs profiling of natural persons, which under the final subparagraph of Article 6(3) always makes an Annex III system high-risk. Nothing here engages the prohibitions in Article 5, in particular no inference of emotions of natural persons in education institutions under Article 5(1)(f), so the deployer should proceed on the basis that the system is high-risk and, where students interact with it directly, observe the Article 50(1) duty that natural persons be informed they are interacting with an AI system.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Annex III point 3(c) - assessing appropriate level of education a person will receive/access
Article 6(3) derogation for narrow/preparatory/non-influencing tasks would otherwise apply given the non-binding recommendation
Article 6(3) final subparagraph - Annex III systems are always high-risk if they profile natural persons, overriding the derogation

rows.question: We manufactured an industrial robot with an embedded AI module that decides when to reduce speed near human workers to prevent hurting them. The robot is covered by the Machinery Regulation, listed in Annex I of the AI Act. We already underwent conformity assessment with a notified body and got a CE mark for the robot. Do we need the AI module undergo a separate AI Act conformity assessment dedicated to the AI Act? Do we need to submit the system to the EU database of high-risk AI systems?
rows.answer: No separate AI Act conformity assessment is required. Under Article 43(3), for a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, such as the Machinery Regulation, the AI Act assessment is integrated into the relevant sectoral third-party conformity assessment procedure, so the notified body verifies the Chapter III Section 2 requirements within that single procedure. That means the existing notified-body assessment must actually have covered the AI module's compliance with those requirements; if it did not, the sectoral assessment has to be completed or supplemented accordingly, and under Article 43(4) any substantial modification to the AI module triggers a new conformity assessment. No registration in the EU database is required either, because the database established under Article 71 covers high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2), namely the Annex III use-case route, and this robot's embedded AI module is high-risk via the Annex I product route under Article 6(1).

criteria.criterion: No
AI Act Section 2 requirements incorporated into existing Machinery Regulation conformity assessment, not a separate AI Act procedure (Article 43(3))
No EU database registration, since Article 71 applies only to Annex III high-risk systems, not Article 6(1)/Annex I product-related ones

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No. The final subparagraph of Article 43(3) is explicit: where a legal act listed in Section A of Annex I, the Union harmonisation legislation covering products such as machinery, lifts and medical devices, permits the product manufacturer to opt out of a third-party conformity assessment on the basis of having applied all harmonised standards, that option may be used only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications covering all requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2. The requirements of Section 2 therefore continue to apply in full to the AI safety component, and Article 43(3) makes them part of the sectoral assessment rather than a separable exercise. Using the opt-out without standards-based coverage of the risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity requirements is non-compliant, and any substantial modification triggers a new conformity assessment under Article 43(4).

criteria.criterion: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones

rows.question: A private contractor runs a region's gas supply service on behalf of the local government. It licenses an AI system from a vendor, fine-tunes it on local data, and then puts it into service under its own brand. To learn about correct applicable classifications of the system and the contractor, what material of the AI Act should I read? Does fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) applies?
rows.answer: No fundamental rights impact assessment is required. Article 27(1) obliges deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, to assess the impact on fundamental rights before deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), but it expressly excepts systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, which is the critical infrastructure area covering the management and operation of the supply of gas. For the classification questions the contractor should read Article 6, which sets the high-risk classification rules, together with point 2 of Annex III, since the system is high-risk only where it operates as a safety component of that critical infrastructure. On its own role it should read Article 25, under which a deployer that puts a high-risk AI system into service under its own name or trade mark, or makes a substantial modification such as fine-tuning on local data, becomes the provider and assumes the full provider obligations, while the vendor that initially placed the system on the market ceases to be its provider and must cooperate and supply the information and technical access needed for compliance.

criteria.criterion: Annex III, point 2 together with Article 6(2) — system classified high-risk as a safety component in gas supply (critical infrastructure)
Article 25(1)(a) — contractor deemed the provider by putting its own name/trademark on the system already placed on the market or put into service
No
FRIA (Article 27) is a deployer obligation; having been reclassified as provider under Article 25(1)(a), the contractor is not acting as deployer of this system

rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).

criteria.criterion: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)

rows.question: Does the obligation to indicate that deep-fakes are artificially generated apply when prosecuting a criminal offence?
rows.answer: No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

criteria.criterion: No
Deep-fake disclosure exemption covers detection, prevention, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences

rows.question: When the intended use of an AI system is listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act, the AI system is automatically high-risk, isn't it? If not, can you explain when that is not the case?
rows.answer: Not always. Under Article 6(2) a system is high-risk only where it falls within one of the lettered use cases listed under the eight Annex III areas of biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes, so a system that merely touches an area heading without matching a listed use case is not caught. Even where a use case is matched, the Article 6(3) derogation removes the system from the high-risk tier where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and it performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or performs a preparatory task to an Annex III assessment. That derogation never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk. The provider must document this assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service.

criteria.criterion: No
Exception applies where system does not pose significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing outcome of decision making

Exception requires one of: narrow procedural task; improving result of previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing/influencing human assessment; preparatory task to an Annex III assessment
Exception never applies (system is always high-risk) if it performs profiling of natural persons

rows.turn1_answer: Not always. Under Article 6(2) a system falling within one of the use cases listed in Annex III is high-risk as a rule, but Article 6(3) provides a derogation: such a system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and it fulfils one of four conditions, namely that it is intended to perform a narrow procedural task, to improve the result of a previously completed human activity, to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review, or to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. That derogation never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk. A provider relying on Article 6(3) must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and the system must still be registered in the EU database under Article 49.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No, the AI system is not "medium risk"; it is high-risk, because the EU AI Act does not mirror the medical device risk classes and instead applies its own tiers. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk where both conditions are met: it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Both limbs are satisfied here, so the device's own "medium-risk" class is legally irrelevant to the AI classification, which is binary rather than graduated. Article 43(3) then integrates the AI Act assessment into the sectoral procedure, so the medical device notified body controls conformity with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements as part of a single conformity assessment.

criteria.criterion: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification

rows.turn1_answer: The AI system is high-risk, and there is no "medium risk" tier in the Regulation, so the medical device's own MDR classification does not carry across as a risk tier for the AI system. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, and where that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment; both conditions are met here. The practical consequence is procedural rather than a separate tier: under Article 43(3) the provider follows the sectoral conformity assessment procedure, meaning the medical device notified-body assessment absorbs the Chapter III Section 2 requirements into a single assessment. The device's medium-risk class determines only which sectoral procedure applies, not whether the AI system is high-risk.

rows.question: Does the EU AI Act explicitly requires to use explainable AI techniques such as LIME or SHAP to increase the trustworthiness of high-risk AI systems?
rows.answer: No, the EU AI Act mandates no specific explainable-AI technique such as LIME or SHAP, and Article 13 instead requires only that high-risk AI systems be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret their output. Article 14 requires effective human oversight, and Article 15 requires appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.

criteria.criterion: No
Article 13 requires sufficient transparency/interpretability for deployers, without naming a technique
Requirement is outcome-based and technology-neutral, leaving choice of method to the provider

Article 14 requires effective human oversight, and Article 15 requires appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.

rows.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to AI systems or AI models or both?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk.

criteria.criterion: Both AI systems and AI models
Art 2(1)(a): providers placing/putting into service AI systems
Art 2(1)(a): providers placing general-purpose AI models on the market

rows.turn1_answer: The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: Biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be is neither prohibited nor high-risk. Article 5, which exhaustively lists the prohibited AI practices, does not cover it, and point 1(a) of Annex III expressly excludes AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification with that sole purpose from the remote biometric identification systems it classifies as high-risk. Such a system would nevertheless become high-risk if it is put to a further use falling within another Annex III point, such as biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes or emotion recognition under points 1(b) and 1(c), or if it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I under Article 6(1). Deployment remains subject to Union data protection law governing the processing of biometric data.

criteria.criterion: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion

rows.turn1_answer: Not prohibited, and not high-risk. Article 5 exhaustively lists the prohibited practices, and biometric verification confined to confirming that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be is none of them, as it neither categorises natural persons to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, nor identifies persons remotely. Annex III likewise does not capture one-to-one biometric verification, since its biometrics area covers remote biometric identification, biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes, and emotion recognition, so the Article 6(2) route is not engaged either. The system would nonetheless be high-risk under Article 6(1) if it were used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I that must undergo a third-party conformity assessment; failing that, it remains subject only to the Article 50 transparency obligations where it interacts directly with natural persons.

rows.question: Are AI safety components within medical devices of MDR class IIa, IIb, or III considered to be high-risk according to the EU AI Act? Why?
rows.answer: AI safety components within medical devices of MDR class IIa, IIb or III are high-risk. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where both conditions are met: it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service. Annex I lists Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, and classes IIa, IIb and III each require notified body involvement under that Regulation, so both limbs are satisfied irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the device. The classification holds regardless of the Annex III route in Article 6(2), which operates in addition to, not instead of, the Annex I product safety route.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Condition: AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (the MDR)
Condition: that product must undergo third-party (notified body) conformity assessment to be placed on the market (Article 6(1))
MDR classes IIa, IIb, III require notified-body conformity assessment, so both cumulative conditions are met

rows.turn1_answer: An AI safety component within a medical device classified as MDR class IIa, IIb, or III is high-risk under Article 6(1), which classifies an AI system as high-risk where it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment. Annex I lists Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, and classes IIa, IIb and III each require notified body involvement under that Regulation, so both conditions of Article 6(1) are satisfied irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the device. Class I devices without a notified body route would not meet the second condition and would therefore fall outside Article 6(1). The conformity assessment follows Article 43, under which providers of such systems follow the relevant procedure required by the medical devices Regulation, with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment.

rows.question: What documentation does a provider of a high-risk AI system needs to keep available for the national competent authorities, and for how long?
rows.answer: Under Article 18, for ten years after the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service, the provider must keep at the disposal of the national competent authorities the technical documentation (Article 11), the quality-management-system documentation (Article 17), the documentation of any changes approved by notified bodies, the decisions and other documents issued by notified bodies, and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47). Separately, under Article 19 the automatically generated logs must be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months.

Quality management system documentation (Article 17)
Notified body change documentation and decisions/other documents, where applicable
EU declaration of conformity (Article 47)
10 years after the system is placed on the market or put into service

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Article 14 governs human oversight, requiring that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use, in order to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights arising in intended use or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse. The oversight measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and are delivered either as measures built into the system by the provider before it is placed on the market or put into service, or as measures identified by the provider for implementation by the deployer. The measures must enable the individuals assigned to oversight to understand the system's capabilities and limitations and monitor its operation, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret its output, decide not to use the system or disregard, override or reverse its output, and intervene or interrupt it through a stop button or similar procedure. For remote biometric identification systems under point 1(a) of Annex III, Article 14(5) additionally bars the deployer from acting on an identification unless it has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority, save where Union or national law considers that requirement disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, asylum or border control authorities.

criteria.criterion: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system

On the deployer side, Article 26 requires human oversight to be assigned to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support.

rows.question: What is the meaning and purpose of 'testing data' in the context of AI systems, and why is it important that it is not leaked during the training process?
rows.answer: Testing data is defined in Article 3(32) as data used to provide an independent evaluation of the AI system, in order to confirm its expected performance before it is placed on the market or put into service. If testing data leaks into the training process, the system is in effect assessed on data it has already seen, which inflates its apparent performance and defeats the purpose of the independent check that Article 10 requires for the datasets of a high-risk AI system.

It must meet the Article 10(3) quality criteria: relevant, sufficiently representative, to the best extent possible free of errors, complete, and with appropriate statistical properties for the intended purpose

Leakage of training data into the testing set destroys the set's independence, so it can no longer reliably verify Article 10(3) compliance and instead yields inflated, misleading accuracy that masks errors, biases or gaps

rows.question: What are the high-risk uses of AI systems listed under 'Administration of justice and democratic processes' cited in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Annex III point 8 lists two high-risk use cases under administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex III point 8(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by a judicial authority, or on its behalf, to assist in researching and interpreting facts and the law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts, or to be used similarly in alternative dispute resolution. Annex III point 8(b) covers AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, with a carve-out for tools that only organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.

Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk

rows.question: Which AI systems used in education or vocational training should be classified as high-risk according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Four use cases are high-risk under point 3 of Annex III (education and vocational training), which Article 6(2) makes high-risk classification turn on: AI systems intended to determine access or admission to, or to assign natural persons to, educational and vocational training institutions at all levels, systems to evaluate learning outcomes including where those outcomes steer the learning process, systems to assess the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or be able to access, and systems for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests. Article 6(3) removes such a system from the high-risk tier where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, but it remains high-risk whenever it profiles natural persons, and the provider must document that self-assessment before placing the system on the market. Separately, an AI system used in this sector is also high-risk under Article 6(1) where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment.

criteria.criterion: Access, admission, or assignment to educational/vocational training institutions at all levels
Evaluating learning outcomes, including to steer the learning process
Assessing the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or can access
Monitoring/detecting prohibited student behaviour during tests

Under the Article 6(3) derogation, such a system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it remains high-risk, and the provider must document that assessment before placing the system on the market. An education AI system may also be high-risk by the separate Article 6(1) route where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment.

rows.question: What obligations, if any, does the EU AI Act set in place for AI systems that interact directly with natural persons? What exceptions, if any, apply?
rows.answer: Yes, a transparency obligation applies. Under Article 50(1), providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the persons concerned are informed they are interacting with an AI system, and that information must be given in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction and in conformity with applicable accessibility requirements. Two limits apply: no disclosure is required where the AI nature is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect natural person in the circumstances and context of use, and the obligation does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties. That law enforcement exception is itself reversed where the system is available for the public to report a criminal offence, in which case the disclosure duty applies in full.

criteria.criterion: Obligation: providers must design/develop the system so natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system
Exception: not required where obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, given the circumstances and context of use

Exception: AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to safeguards for third parties' rights and freedoms — unless available for the public to report a criminal offence

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices listed in Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, where the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, under Article 99(3). This is the highest of the three ceilings in Article 99, which sets fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % for breaches of the listed operator and notified-body obligations and up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or competent authorities. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) caps the fine at the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount, and all penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive and take account of the gravity and nature of the infringement. Where the offender is a Union institution, body, office or agency, Article 100 instead empowers the European Data Protection Supervisor to impose fines of up to EUR 1 500 000 for infringements of the Article 5 prohibited practices.

criteria.criterion: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices

rows.turn1_answer: Non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibited practices attracts the highest tier of administrative fines under Article 99(3): up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. This ceiling applies to any of the eight prohibited practices, namely subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, social scoring, individual criminal-offence risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits, untargeted scraping of facial images for facial recognition databases, emotion recognition in the workplace and education institutions, biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Under Article 99(6) the ceiling for SMEs, including start-ups, is the lower of the fixed amount or the turnover percentage, and penalties must in every case be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, taking account of the gravity and nature of the infringement. Where the offender is a Union institution, body, office or agency, Article 100(2) instead empowers the European Data Protection Supervisor to impose administrative fines of up to EUR 1 500 000 for non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibition.

rows.question: How does Annex II relate to prohibited uses of AI systems?
rows.answer: Annex II does not itself prohibit anything. It functions as a closed list that narrows one exception to a prohibited practice: Article 5 prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, and Article 5(1)(h)(iii) permits such use only to localise or identify a person suspected of an Annex II offence, and only where that offence is punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years. The Annex II offences are terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, illicit trafficking in weapons munitions or explosives, murder, grievous bodily injury, illicit trade in human organs or tissue, illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials, kidnapping illegal restraint or hostage-taking, crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships, rape, environmental crime, organised or armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of those offences. Annex II is irrelevant to the other Article 5 prohibited practices and to the two remaining Article 5(1)(h) objectives, namely the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and for missing persons, and the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable terrorist attack.

Referenced in Article 5(1)(h)(iii) as basis for one exception to the Article 5(1)(h) prohibition on 'real-time' remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement
Exception (localising/identifying a suspect) applies only if the offence is listed in Annex II and punishable by a custodial sentence/detention order of max at least four years

rows.question: Can the European Commission amend Annex III of the EU AI Act to add or modify use-cases classified as high-risk AI systems? Under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes, the Commission may amend Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases of high-risk AI systems, but only through delegated acts adopted in accordance with Article 97 and only where two cumulative conditions in Article 7(1) are both met: the AI systems are intended to be used in one of the areas already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk posed by the high-risk AI systems already listed there. In assessing that second condition the Commission must weigh the criteria in Article 7(2), including the intended purpose, the extent of use, the nature and amount of data processed, the degree of autonomy, the severity and reversibility of harm, and the availability of effective measures of redress or of measures preventing or substantially minimising the risks. Procedurally, Article 97 confers this power for five years from 1 August 2024 with tacit extension unless opposed, requires the Commission to consult experts designated by each Member State before adoption, and lets the act enter into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within three months of notification, extendable by a further three months, with revocation possible at any time. The same delegated-act power under Article 7(3) allows removal of a use-case from Annex III only where it no longer poses any significant risk to fundamental rights, health or safety and the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection under Union law.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Condition: AI intended to be used in any of the areas listed in Annex III
Condition: posed risk is equal or greater than those already referred to in Annex III
Both conditions must apply ("and" clause)

Article 7(1) empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts amending Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases of high-risk AI systems where two conditions are fulfilled cumulatively: the AI systems are intended to be used in one of the areas already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk posed by the high-risk AI systems already referred to in Annex III. The Commission cannot create a new area, and in assessing the second condition it must weigh the criteria in Article 7(2), including the intended purpose, the extent of use, the nature and amount of data processed, the degree of autonomy, the severity and reversibility of harm, and the availability of effective measures of redress or of measures to prevent or substantially minimise those risks. rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful.

criteria.criterion: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person

rows.question: Should market surveilance authorities be provided with remote access to documentations and data sets used to develop a high-risk AI system?
rows.answer: Yes, where relevant and limited to what is necessary to fulfil their tasks, providers must grant market surveillance authorities full access to the documentation and to the training, validation and testing data sets used to develop a high-risk AI system, including, where appropriate and subject to security safeguards, through application programming interfaces (API) or other relevant technical means and tools enabling remote access, under Article 74, which governs market surveillance of AI systems. Access to the source code is a separate and narrower power under the same Article, granted only upon a reasoned request and only where such access is necessary to assess conformity with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements and where testing, auditing and verification based on the data and documentation already provided have been exhausted or proved insufficient. Any information or documentation so obtained is subject to the confidentiality obligations of Article 78.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Full access to documentation and to training, validation and testing data sets, granted by providers, limited to what is necessary for the authority's tasks
Remote access (e.g. via API or other technical means) permitted only "where appropriate" and subject to security safeguards

rows.turn1_answer: Yes, where remote access is appropriate and subject to security safeguards. Article 74 requires providers to grant market surveillance authorities full access to the documentation as well as the training, validation and testing data sets used for the development of high-risk AI systems, including through application programming interfaces (API) or other relevant technical means and tools enabling remote access, where relevant and limited to what is necessary to fulfil those authorities' tasks. Access to the source code is a narrower power under the same Article, available only upon a reasoned request and only where such access is necessary to assess conformity with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements and where verification based on the data and documentation already provided has been exhausted or proved insufficient. Any information or documentation so obtained is subject to the confidentiality obligations of Article 78.

rows.question: If a provider of a high-risk AI system confirms that the system achieves an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity at the time of development, then no further action is required by the provider on these aspects in the future. Correct?
rows.answer: No. Article 15 requires high-risk AI systems to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and to perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle, so the duty is continuing rather than satisfied once at development, and it extends to resilience against errors, faults or inconsistencies through technical redundancy such as back-up plans or fail-safe mechanisms, and to resilience against unauthorised third parties exploiting vulnerabilities to alter use, outputs or performance. That continuing performance must be maintained through the risk management system under Article 9, which is a documented iterative process maintained across the lifecycle, requiring identification of foreseeable risks, evaluation of risks under intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse, and testing to ensure consistent performance. The quality management system under Article 17 reinforces this by requiring examination, test and validation procedures before, during and after development at a defined frequency, together with a strategy for managing modifications to the system. The declared levels of accuracy and accuracy metrics under Article 15(3) and Article 13(3)(b)(ii), including known and foreseeable circumstances affecting expected accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, must remain accurate in the instructions for use.

Must perform consistently throughout lifecycle, including resilience to errors/faults/inconsistencies (Art. 15(1),(4))
Cybersecurity resilience against third-party exploitation is ongoing, not one-time (Art. 15(5))
Accuracy levels/metrics must be declared in instructions of use (Art. 15(3))

rows.turn1_answer: No. Article 15 requires high-risk AI systems to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and to perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle, so the duty is continuing rather than discharged at development. It is sustained by the risk management system under Article 9, which must be established, implemented, documented and maintained across the lifecycle and updated in light of testing and residual risk evaluation, and by the quality management system under Article 17, whose examination, test and validation procedures run before, during and after development. The declared levels of accuracy, accuracy metrics, robustness and cybersecurity must also be stated in the instructions for use under Article 13(3)(b)(ii), together with any known and foreseeable circumstances that may affect those expected levels.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems have no mandatory duties under the Act, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

criteria.criterion: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)

rows.question: Does "systemic risk" apply to AI systems or general purpose AI models or both?
rows.answer: Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.

Systemic risk classification applies only to general-purpose AI models (Article 51), not to AI systems

rows.question: Are AI systems that fall under one of the areas of Annex III, but not falling within a use-case within such areas, considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Falling within one of the eight areas of Annex III is not sufficient, because Article 6(2) classifies a system as high-risk only where it corresponds to one of the lettered use-cases listed under those numbered area headings, which cover biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. A system that operates in such an area but performs none of the listed use-cases is outside the Annex III route, though it may still be high-risk under Article 6(1) where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I that must undergo a third-party conformity assessment. Conversely, a system that does match a listed use-case is presumed high-risk unless the provider documents, before placing it on the market, that it poses no significant risk of harm under one of the Article 6(3) conditions, namely a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or a preparatory task, and it never performs profiling of natural persons.

criteria.criterion: No
High-risk requires falling within a specific enumerated use case listed in Annex III, not merely within the broader area grouping those use cases
Annex III areas are organisational headings; the operative trigger is the individual use-case description

rows.turn1_answer: No. An AI system is high-risk under the Annex III route only where it falls within one of the lettered use-cases listed under one of the eight areas of Annex III, since Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk the AI systems referred to in Annex III rather than every system operating in an area covered by a numbered heading. rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))

rows.question: If I have an AI system that is high-risk because listed in the use cases of Annex III, and change it to a different use case that is not in Annex I or III, does it stay high-risk due to its historical provenance?
rows.answer: No, classification is forward-looking and attaches to the system's intended purpose, not to its history. Under Article 6(2) an AI system is high-risk because it falls within one of the use cases listed in Annex III, which enumerates eight areas covering biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Once the intended purpose is changed to a use case outside Annex III, and the system is neither a safety component of, nor itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), it is no longer high-risk. The prior classification confers no residual high-risk status, though the change of intended purpose must be genuine and reflected in the system's documented intended purpose rather than nominal.

criteria.criterion: No
High-risk status under Article 6 depends on the AI system's current intended purpose/use case, not its prior classification
If the new use case falls outside both Annex I and Annex III, neither condition in Article 6(1) or 6(2) is met, so the system is not high-risk

rows.turn1_answer: No, classification does not attach to a system's history. Article 6 classifies an AI system by its intended purpose at the time it is placed on the market or put into service, through two routes: Article 6(1), covering systems that are a safety component of, or themselves are, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment, and Article 6(2), covering systems falling within one of the lettered use cases listed under the eight areas of Annex III. Where the new intended purpose falls outside both Annex I and any Annex III use case, the system is no longer high-risk, and the fact that an earlier version of it was classified high-risk has no continuing effect. Conversely, a system that still falls under an Annex III use case remains high-risk unless it satisfies the Article 6(3) derogation for a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or a preparatory task, and never where it performs profiling of natural persons, with the provider documenting that assessment before placing the system on the market.

rows.question: How are AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum classified, and what exception is given for certain campaign-related tools?
rows.answer: Under Annex III point 8(b), AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum, or the voting behaviour of natural persons in exercising their vote, are high-risk under Article 6(2). Annex III point 8(b) itself excludes systems to whose output natural persons are not directly exposed, such as tools used only to organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view, which therefore fall outside this high-risk category.

Covers AI systems influencing election/referendum outcome or voters' voting behaviour
Exception: AI systems whose output natural persons are not directly exposed to are excluded
Example given: tools organising/optimising/structuring political campaigns administratively or logistically

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Article 1 states that the purpose of the Regulation is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation. To that end, Article 1 lays down harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service and the use of AI systems in the Union, prohibitions of certain AI practices, specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems, harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems, harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models, rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement, and measures to support innovation with a particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups.

criteria.criterion: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which specific AI systems are explicitly listed as high-risk because they make decisions in critical life- and health-related situations involving emergency calls and triage?
rows.answer: Under Annex III point 5(d), AI systems intended to be used for dispatching or prioritising in dispatching emergency first-response services, or for triage of emergency medical-service patients (including by fire brigades and medical aid), are explicitly listed as high-risk. They fall within the 'essential private and public services' category of the eight Annex III high-risk use cases and are classified as high-risk through the Annex III route of Article 6(2), which treats any system falling within a listed use case as high-risk.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as part of their supervisory role for an AI regulatory sandbox, compliance with which specific Article must the market surveillance authority verify?
rows.answer: Article 60. Where testing in real world conditions is carried out for AI systems supervised within an AI regulatory sandbox, the market surveillance authority must verify compliance with Article 60, which permits real-world testing of high-risk AI systems subject to an approved real-world testing plan, informed consent of test subjects, registration, and market surveillance oversight. That verification duty forms part of the authority's supervisory role for the sandbox under Article 76, which gives market surveillance authorities the competences and powers to ensure real-world testing conforms to the Regulation. The authority may, as appropriate, allow the provider or prospective provider to conduct that testing in derogation from the conditions in Article 60(4), points (f) and (g).

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions: it performs a narrow procedural task, it improves the result of a previously completed human activity, it detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or it performs a preparatory task. Under Article 6(3), this exception never applies where the system profiles natural persons. The provider must document the assessment before placing the system on the market and register it under Article 49(2).

rows.question: Is an AI system used to detect decision-making patterns or deviations for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: Even within an Annex III use case, Article 6(3)(c) provides that an AI system intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm and is not meant to replace or influence a previously completed human assessment without proper human review. However, under Article 6(3) such a system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons.

rows.question: Regarding the European Artificial Intelligence Board: (1) Who designates its members? (2) How long is the term? How many times is the term renewable? (3) must members represent stakeholder interests or act impartially/objectively? (4) what voting threshold is required to adopt the Board's rules of procedure (is a simple 50%+1 majority enough)?
rows.answer: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (Article 65) has one representative per Member State, each serving a three-year term renewable once under Article 65(3). Under Article 65(4) each is their Member State's single contact point rather than an independent stakeholder appointee, while Article 65(7) requires the Board to safeguard the objectivity and impartiality of its activities. Its rules of procedure are adopted by a two-thirds majority under Article 65(5), so a simple majority is not sufficient.

Two-thirds majority required to adopt rules of procedure (simple majority not enough)

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine on a provider of a general-purpose AI model under Article 101, the provision under which the Commission may fine such providers up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for infringements of their Chapter V obligations, for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, or for failing to comply with a requested measure. Exercising that unlimited jurisdiction, the Court may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed. Before the Commission adopts such a decision it must communicate its preliminary findings to the provider and give it an opportunity to be heard, and any fine must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

rows.question: Consider the situation in which a market surveillance authority (MSA) determines that an AI system, originally classified as non-high-risk by the provider, is in fact high-risk. Does the provider need to recall and suspend the use of the system without undue delay, or does the MSA provide a timeframe within which the provider can take corrective actions? Or does this depend on the gravity of the situation?
rows.answer: The market surveillance authority sets a period; immediate recall is not automatic. Under Article 80, which governs AI systems the provider classified as non-high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation, the authority first evaluates the classification and, on finding the system high-risk, must without undue delay require the provider to bring it into compliance with the requirements and obligations of the Regulation and to take appropriate corrective action within a period the authority may prescribe, with fines under Article 99 where the provider misses that period or misclassified the system to circumvent Chapter III, Section 2. Gravity determines the length and the escalation: where the system also presents a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, the Article 79 procedure sets the corrective period, to withdraw, recall or bring into compliance, at the shorter of the period prescribed or 15 working days, and if adequate corrective action is not taken in time Article 79(5) to (9) applies, allowing the authority to impose provisional measures prohibiting, restricting, withdrawing or recalling the system. Independently of any authority deadline, Article 20 obliges a provider that considers or has reason to consider a high-risk AI system already placed on the market not to be in conformity to take the necessary corrective actions immediately, namely bringing it into conformity, withdrawing, disabling or recalling it, and to inform distributors, deployers, the authorised representative and importers, and to inform the market surveillance authorities where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1).

Provider must bring the system into compliance and take corrective action within that MSA-prescribed period (Article 80(2) and 80(4))
Failure to comply within that period triggers fines under Article 99 (and Article 79(5)-(9) applies), not gravity-based variation of the timeframe

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what presumption applies when a high-risk AI system is trained and tested on data that reflects the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which it is intended to be used?
rows.answer: A presumption of conformity applies: under Article 42(1), a high-risk AI system trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting within which it is intended to be used is presumed to comply with the relevant requirements of Article 10(4), which requires data sets to take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements particular to that setting. The presumption is confined to Article 10(4) and does not extend to the other data governance duties in Article 10, such as the data governance and management practices under Article 10(2) or the relevance, representativeness, error-freedom and completeness criteria under Article 10(3). Article 42(2) supplies a separate presumption, whereby high-risk AI systems certified, or for which a statement of conformity has been issued, under a cybersecurity scheme pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2019/881 with references published in the Official Journal are presumed to comply with the cybersecurity requirements of Article 15, in so far as that certificate or statement covers those requirements.

criteria.criterion: Presumed compliant with Article 10(3) representativeness/quality requirement for that setting
Presumption is limited to the extent required by the intended purpose
Not an exemption from other Article 10 obligations (e.g., bias examination/mitigation)

This presumption of conformity is established by Article 42(1). rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: Before placing a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III on the market or putting it into service, the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative must register themselves and the system in the EU database that the Commission sets up and maintains under Article 71, entering the data listed in Section A of Annex VIII (Article 49). That information is the name, address and contact details of the provider, the same details of any person submitting on the provider's behalf, the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative where applicable, the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability, a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported, a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic, the status of the AI system (on the market or in service, no longer placed on the market or in service, recalled), the type, number and expiry date of the certificate issued by the notified body with that body's name or identification number where applicable, a scanned copy of that certificate, any Member States in which the system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available in the Union, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity drawn up under Article 47, electronic instructions for use, and an optional URL for additional information. Electronic instructions for use are not submitted for high-risk AI systems in the areas of law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management referred to in Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7, and for those systems registration is made in a secure non-public section of the database limited to the items identified in Article 49(4). High-risk AI systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III are registered at national level rather than in the EU database.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what is an "AI regulatory sandbox"? Provide the definition elements (what it is, who sets it up, for whom it is intended, to do what, for how long).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what transparency obligation applies to deployers when they use an AI system to generate or manipulate text for the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest, and what are the two exceptions where this obligation does not apply?
rows.answer: Under Article 50(4), a deployer that uses an AI system to generate or manipulate text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated. Under Article 50(4), that disclosure duty does not apply in two cases: first, where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; and second, where the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication of the content.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. rows.question:
Under the EU AI Act, must an employer inform affected workers and workers' representatives before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system in the workplace?
If so, should possibly specific rules or procedures be followed to provide this information?
rows.answer: Yes. rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what specific information must a provider/prospective provider submit (and keep up to date) regarding testing of a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside an AI regulatory sandbox?
rows.answer: Five items must be registered and thereafter kept up to date under Annex IX, which sets the information to be submitted upon registration of testing in real world conditions of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III: a Union-wide unique single identification number of the testing, the name and contact details of the provider or prospective provider and of the deployers involved, a brief description of the AI system, its intended purpose and other information necessary to identify it, a summary of the main characteristics of the plan for testing in real world conditions, and information on the suspension or termination of the testing. Article 60 also requires the provider or prospective provider to notify that market surveillance authority of any suspension or termination of the testing and of the final outcomes.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, if a deployer has reason to believe that the use of a high-risk AI system may present a risk, what must the deployer do, and whom must the deployer inform?
rows.answer: Where a deployer has reason to consider that use of the high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions for use may result in that system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), Article 26(5) requires the deployer to inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority without undue delay, and to suspend the use of that system. That duty sits within the same paragraph's obligation to monitor the operation of the system on the basis of the instructions for use and, where relevant, to inform providers in accordance with the post-market monitoring arrangements of Article 72. Where the deployer has identified a serious incident, it must also immediately inform first the provider, and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities, with Article 73 reporting applying mutatis mutandis if the provider cannot be reached. This reporting obligation does not cover sensitive operational data of deployers that are law enforcement authorities, and deployers must in any event cooperate with the competent authorities in any action taken in relation to the system under Article 26(12).
