rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Article 13 requires high-risk AI systems to be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret and appropriately use their output, and to be accompanied by instructions for use in an appropriate digital format or otherwise containing concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers. Under Article 13(3) those instructions must contain at least six categories: the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the system, the changes to the system and its performance pre-determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment, if any, the human oversight measures including the technical measures facilitating interpretation of outputs, the computational and hardware resources needed together with the expected lifetime and any necessary maintenance and care measures including their frequency and software updates, and, where relevant, a description of the mechanisms allowing deployers to properly collect, store and interpret the logs. The performance category under Article 13(3)(b) itself covers seven elements: the intended purpose, the level of accuracy including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity against which the system has been tested and validated and any known and foreseeable circumstances affecting those expected levels, any known or foreseeable circumstance in intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse that may lead to risks to health and safety or fundamental rights, where applicable the technical capabilities and characteristics for providing information relevant to explaining the output, when appropriate the performance regarding specific persons or groups on which the system is intended to be used, when appropriate specifications for the input data or other information on the training, validation and testing data sets used, and where applicable information enabling deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately. This information also serves the deployer's own duties, since Article 26 requires deployers to use and monitor the system in accordance with the instructions for use and to assign human oversight to competent, trained and authorised natural persons.

criteria.criterion: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant

rows.turn1_answer: Under Article 13, which requires high-risk AI systems to be sufficiently transparent and to be accompanied by instructions for use containing concise, complete, correct and clear information, the provider must supply six categories of information. Those are the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the system, any changes to the system and its performance pre-determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment, the human oversight measures referred to in Article 14 including the technical measures facilitating interpretation of outputs, the computational and hardware resources needed together with the expected lifetime and any necessary maintenance and care measures including their frequency and software updates, and, where relevant, a description of the mechanisms allowing deployers properly to collect, store and interpret the logs kept under Article 12 on record-keeping. The performance category itself covers the intended purpose, the level of accuracy including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity against which the system was tested and validated plus circumstances affecting those expected levels, any known or foreseeable circumstance under intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse that may create risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, where applicable the technical capabilities to provide information relevant to explain the output, when appropriate performance regarding specific persons or groups on which the system is intended to be used, when appropriate specifications for the input data and information on the training, validation and testing data sets, and where applicable information enabling deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately. These are minimum contents, and the deployer relies on them to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use and to monitor its operation under Article 26.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what actions must a provider take when it considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation?
rows.answer: The provider must act immediately under Article 20, which imposes the corrective action and duty of information obligation. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity with the Regulation must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring that system into conformity, to withdraw it, to disable it, or to recall it, as appropriate, and must inform the distributors of the system concerned and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and importers. Where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), which governs AI systems presenting a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, Article 20(2) requires the provider, on becoming aware of that risk, to investigate the causes immediately in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and to inform the market surveillance authorities competent for the system and, where applicable, the notified body that issued a certificate for it, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. This duty is also restated in Article 16, which lists the provider's obligations and requires it to take the necessary corrective actions and provide information as required in Article 20.

criteria.criterion: Immediately take necessary corrective action: bring into conformity, withdraw, disable, or recall, as appropriate
Inform distributors of the system concerned
Where applicable, inform deployers, authorised representative and importers accordingly

rows.turn1_answer: The provider must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring the system into conformity, to withdraw it, to disable it, or to recall it, as appropriate, and must inform the distributors of the high-risk AI system concerned and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and importers (Article 20(1), the corrective actions and duty of information obligation). Where the high-risk AI system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), which covers a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights triggering a market surveillance evaluation, and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the market surveillance authorities competent for that system and, where applicable, the notified body that issued its certificate, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken (Article 20(2)). This duty is also listed among the provider obligations in Article 16, which requires providers to take the necessary corrective actions and provide information as required in Article 20.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, what is the definition of (a) a "conformity assessment body" and (b) "conformity assessment"?
rows.answer: Both terms are defined in Article 3, which sets out the definitions applying throughout the Regulation. A "conformity assessment body" means a body that performs third-party conformity assessment activities, including testing, certification and inspection, and such a body becomes a "notified body" once it is notified in accordance with the Regulation and other relevant Union harmonisation legislation. "Conformity assessment" means the process of demonstrating whether the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 relating to a high-risk AI system have been fulfilled. That process is operationalised by Article 43, which requires providers of high-risk AI systems to follow either the internal control procedure in Annex VI or the quality management system and technical documentation procedure involving a notified body in Annex VII.

Conformity assessment body: activities include testing, certification and inspection
Conformity assessment: the process of demonstrating whether the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements for a high-risk AI system have been fulfilled

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, including with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations such as civil society organisations and academia, and a single code may cover one or more AI systems having a similar intended purpose (Article 95(3)). The bodies that must encourage and facilitate their drawing up are the AI Office and the Member States, in respect of codes fostering voluntary application to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems of some or all of the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 (Article 95(1)). The AI Office and the Member States must also take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, when encouraging and facilitating that drawing up (Article 95(4)).

criteria.criterion: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct

rows.turn1_answer: Codes of conduct under Article 95 may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, including with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations such as civil society organisations and academia. The AI Office and the Member States are the bodies that must encourage and facilitate their drawing up, in particular to foster the voluntary application to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems of some or all of the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, and they must take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, when doing so. A single code of conduct may cover one or more AI systems, taking into account the similarity of the intended purpose of the relevant systems.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which AI systems in the financial services area are classified as high-risk under Annex III(5)(b), and what explicit exceptions are listed?
rows.answer: High-risk covers AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or to establish their credit score, with the single explicit exception of AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud, which Annex III point 5(b) carves out of that use-case. Annex III point 5 sits in the area of access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits, and under the Annex III route in Article 6(2) a system is high-risk only where it falls within one of the lettered use-cases listed there. A creditworthiness or credit scoring system nonetheless escapes high-risk classification under the Article 6(3) derogation where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it remains high-risk. A provider relying on that derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service.

criteria.criterion: AI systems evaluating creditworthiness or establishing credit score of natural persons
Exception: AI systems used for detecting financial fraud

rows.turn1_answer: High-risk, subject to one explicit carve-out. Annex III(5)(b), sitting under the area on access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits, lists as high-risk AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, and the only exception stated in that point is AI systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud. Article 6(2) gives that listing its effect by classifying as high-risk any system falling within a use-case listed in Annex III. Article 6(3) further removes such a system from the high-risk tier where it poses no significant risk of harm because it performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, unless it profiles natural persons, and the provider must document that assessment before the system is placed on the market.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider established outside the EU do in order to place a high-risk AI system on the Union market?
rows.answer: A provider established in a third country must, prior to making the high-risk AI system available on the Union market, appoint by written mandate an authorised representative established in the Union, and must enable that representative to perform the tasks specified in the mandate (Article 22). The mandate must empower the authorised representative to verify that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up and that the appropriate conformity assessment procedure has been carried out, to keep the provider's contact details, the declaration, the technical documentation and any notified body certificate at the disposal of competent authorities for 10 years after the system is placed on the market or put into service, to supply information and documentation on reasoned request including access to the automatically generated logs under the provider's control, to cooperate with competent authorities in action taken on the system, and to comply with or verify the registration obligations (Article 22). The authorised representative may be addressed by competent authorities in addition to or instead of the provider on all compliance issues, and must terminate the mandate and immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority, and where applicable the notified body, if it considers the provider to be acting contrary to the Regulation (Article 22). Appointing a representative does not displace the provider's own substantive duties, which remain fully applicable.

criteria.criterion: Appoint an authorised representative established in the Union, by written mandate
Must occur prior to making the system available on the Union market

Representative empowered per Article 22(3) tasks (verify conformity documentation, retain records 10 years, provide information/log access to authorities, cooperate with authorities, handle registration)

rows.turn1_answer: A provider established in a third country must, prior to making the high-risk AI system available on the Union market, appoint an authorised representative established in the Union by written mandate, and must enable that representative to perform the tasks specified in the mandate (Article 22). The mandate must empower the authorised representative to verify that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up and that an appropriate conformity assessment procedure has been carried out, to keep the provider's contact details, the declaration of conformity, the technical documentation and any notified body certificate at the disposal of competent authorities for 10 years after placing on the market or putting into service, to supply that information and documentation on a reasoned request including access to the automatically generated logs under the provider's control, to cooperate with competent authorities in actions to reduce and mitigate risks, and to comply with or verify the registration obligations under Article 49(1) (Article 22). The authorised representative must also be empowered to be addressed by competent authorities in addition to or instead of the provider on all compliance issues, and must terminate the mandate and immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority if it considers the provider to be acting contrary to the Regulation (Article 22).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Article 17(1) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to put in place a quality management system ensuring compliance with the Regulation, documented in a systematic and orderly manner in written policies, procedures and instructions. It must include at least thirteen elements: a strategy for regulatory compliance including conformity assessment and management of modifications, design, design control and design verification techniques, development, quality control and quality assurance techniques, examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency, technical specifications and standards to be applied, data management systems and procedures, the risk management system of Article 9, the setting-up and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system under Article 72, procedures for reporting a serious incident under Article 73, handling of communication with national competent authorities, notified bodies, other operators and interested parties, record-keeping systems for all relevant documentation, resource management including security of supply, and an accountability framework allocating responsibilities of management and staff. Implementation is proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, without lowering the degree of rigour and level of protection required, and providers already subject to quality management obligations under sectoral Union law may embed these aspects within that system, while financial institutions subject to internal governance requirements under Union financial services law are deemed to comply except as regards the risk management system, post-market monitoring and serious incident reporting elements. Microenterprises without partner or linked enterprises may comply with certain elements in a simplified manner under Article 63, which does not exempt them from the other requirements of the Regulation.

criteria.criterion: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff

rows.turn1_answer: Providers of high-risk AI systems must put in place a quality management system that ensures compliance with the Regulation and is documented in a systematic and orderly manner through written policies, procedures and instructions, covering at least thirteen aspects under Article 17(1). Those aspects are a regulatory compliance strategy including conformity assessment and management of modifications, design, design control and design verification techniques, development, quality control and quality assurance techniques, examination, test and validation procedures before, during and after development and their frequency, technical specifications and standards including the means used where harmonised standards are not applied in full, data management systems and procedures covering acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention, the risk management system referred to in Article 9, the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72, procedures for reporting a serious incident in accordance with Article 73, handling of communication with national competent authorities, notified bodies, other operators, customers and other interested parties, record-keeping systems and procedures for all relevant documentation, resource management including security-of-supply measures, and an accountability framework setting out management and staff responsibilities. Implementation must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation while respecting the degree of rigour and level of protection required, providers already subject to quality management obligations under sectoral Union law may integrate these aspects into that system, and financial institutions complying with internal governance rules under Union financial services law are deemed to fulfil the obligation except for the risk management system, post-market monitoring and serious incident reporting elements. Microenterprises without partner or linked enterprises may comply with certain elements in a simplified manner under Article 63, without affecting the level of protection or their compliance with the high-risk requirements.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what additional obligations apply to providers of a general-purpose AI model that is classified as a model with systemic risk?
rows.answer: Four additional obligations apply under Article 55, on top of the Article 53 duties owed by every general-purpose AI model provider (Annex XI technical documentation, Annex XII information for downstream providers, a copyright policy, and a public training-data summary): performing model evaluation under standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including documented adversarial testing; assessing and mitigating possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, stemming from the development, placing on the market or use of the model; keeping track of, documenting and reporting without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, national competent authorities relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures; and ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Classification triggers a further duty under Article 52 to notify the Commission without delay and in any event within two weeks of meeting, or knowing it will meet, the Article 51 high-impact-capabilities condition presumed at cumulative training compute above 10^25 floating-point operations, with the option to submit substantiated arguments that the model nonetheless presents no systemic risk. The Article 53(2) exemption for models released under a free and open-source licence does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, so the technical documentation and downstream information duties remain owed in full. Compliance may be demonstrated through Article 56 codes of practice until a harmonised standard is published, and any information obtained under Article 55, including trade secrets, is covered by the Article 78 confidentiality obligation.

criteria.criterion: Perform state-of-the-art model evaluation including documented adversarial testing to identify/mitigate systemic risks
Assess and mitigate possible Union-level systemic risks, including their sources
Track, document and report serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office/national competent authorities without undue delay
Ensure adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure

rows.turn1_answer: Four additional obligations apply on top of the Article 53 baseline (technical documentation under Annex XI, downstream-provider information under Annex XII, a copyright policy, and a public training-data summary), which itself cannot be escaped by the free and open-source licence exemption once a model is classified as having systemic risk. Under Article 55, the provider must perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing, assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level including their sources arising from development, placing on the market or use of the model, keep track of, document and report without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures, and ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Separately, Article 52 requires the provider to notify the Commission without delay and in any event within two weeks of meeting, or knowing it will meet, the Article 51 high-impact capabilities condition, presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations, with the option of submitting substantiated arguments that the model exceptionally presents no systemic risk. Compliance may be demonstrated through the codes of practice facilitated by the AI Office under Article 56 until a harmonised standard is published, and any documentation obtained, including trade secrets, is protected by the confidentiality obligations in Article 78.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what are the four grounds on which non-compliance with the Act may be alleged (as listed in Article 79(6))?
rows.answer: Article 79(6) requires the notifying market surveillance authority to indicate whether the alleged non-compliance is due to one or more of four grounds: non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5, a failure of a high-risk AI system to meet the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, shortcomings in the harmonised standards or common specifications referred to in Articles 40 and 41 that confer a presumption of conformity, and non-compliance with Article 50. These grounds form part of the notification of provisional measures under Article 79(5), which must also identify the non-compliant AI system, its origin and supply chain, the nature of the non-compliance and the risk involved, the nature and duration of the national measures, and the arguments put forward by the relevant operator.

criteria.criterion: Non-compliance with prohibition of AI practices under Article 5
Failure of high-risk AI system to meet Chapter III, Section 2 requirements
Shortcomings in harmonised standards/common specifications under Articles 40-41
Non-compliance with Article 50

rows.turn1_answer: Article 79(6) requires the market surveillance authority, when notifying a provisional measure, to indicate whether the non-compliance is due to one or more of four grounds: non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5, a failure of a high-risk AI system to meet the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, shortcomings in the harmonised standards or common specifications referred to in Articles 40 and 41 conferring a presumption of conformity, and non-compliance with Article 50. That indication forms part of a notification that must also identify the non-compliant AI system, its origin and supply chain, the nature of the non-compliance alleged and the risk involved, the nature and duration of the national measures taken, and the arguments put forward by the relevant operator.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Permitted only in three exhaustive situations, all subject to the requirement that the use be strictly necessary for the objective. Article 5(1)(h), which prohibits the use of real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement, allows it for the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings and the search for missing persons, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack, and the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence for the purpose of a criminal investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty, limited to the offences listed in Annex II, namely terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs, weapons and nuclear material, murder, kidnapping, rape, armed robbery, organised crime, participation in a criminal organisation and environmental crime, and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years. Outside that law enforcement context in publicly accessible spaces the practice is not prohibited but classified high-risk, since Annex III point 1(a) lists remote biometric identification systems as a high-risk use case under Article 6(2), excluding biometric verification whose sole purpose is confirming that a person is who they claim to be. Article 5(1)(h) is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for the processing of biometric data for purposes other than law enforcement.

criteria.criterion: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order

rows.turn1_answer: Three exhaustive objectives, and only where the use is strictly necessary: the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings and the search for missing persons; the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; and the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of a criminal investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty, for the offences listed in Annex II (terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs, weapons or nuclear material, murder, kidnapping, rape, armed robbery, organised crime, participation in a criminal organisation, environmental crime) and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years. Outside these carve-outs, Article 5(1)(h) makes the use of real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes a prohibited practice. Each permitted use requires prior authorisation by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, with a duly justified urgency exception under which authorisation must be requested within 24 hours and use stopped immediately if refused, plus notification of the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority. Article 5(1)(h) is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for the processing of biometric data for purposes other than law enforcement.

rows.question: Under Article 32 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, when is a conformity assessment body presumed to comply with the requirements in Article 31?
rows.answer: A conformity assessment body is presumed to comply with Article 31 where it demonstrates its conformity with the criteria laid down in the relevant harmonised standards, or parts thereof, the references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union (Article 32). That presumption extends only in so far as the applicable harmonised standards cover those requirements, so any Article 31 requirement not covered by such a standard must still be demonstrated directly. Article 31 sets the substantive requirements concerned, including establishment under the national law of a Member State with legal personality, independence from the provider and from operators with an economic interest, no direct involvement in the design, development, marketing or use of the high-risk AI systems assessed, documented procedures safeguarding impartiality and confidentiality, appropriate liability insurance unless liability is assumed by the Member State, and permanent availability of sufficient personnel with experience relating to the relevant types of AI systems, data and data computing.

criteria.criterion: Body demonstrates conformity with relevant harmonised standards (or parts thereof)
Condition: references to those standards published in the Official Journal of the European Union
Presumption limited to the extent those standards cover the Article 31 requirements

rows.turn1_answer: A conformity assessment body is presumed to comply with the Article 31 requirements relating to notified bodies where it demonstrates its conformity with the criteria laid down in the relevant harmonised standards, or parts thereof, the references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union (Article 32). That presumption extends only in so far as the applicable harmonised standards cover those requirements, so any Article 31 requirement not covered by such a standard must still be demonstrated separately. Article 31 sets the substantive conditions concerned, including establishment under the national law of a Member State with legal personality, independence and absence of conflicts of interest, documented procedures safeguarding impartiality and confidentiality, appropriate liability insurance unless the Member State assumes that liability, and sufficient permanent personnel with the requisite competence relating to AI systems, data and data computing.

rows.question: Who is entitled to lodge a complaint about an infringement, and to which authority must the complaint be submitted?
rows.answer: Any natural or legal person having grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the Regulation may submit a complaint, and Article 85 requires it to be addressed to the relevant market surveillance authority, which must take it into account in its market surveillance activities and handle it under the dedicated procedures established in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. The right does not depend on the complainant's own rights being affected, and it applies without prejudice to other administrative or judicial remedies. Where the alleged infringement concerns a Union institution, body, office or agency, the European Data Protection Supervisor is the authority empowered under Article 100 to impose administrative fines on that entity.

criteria.criterion: Any natural or legal person
Grounds to consider there has been an infringement of the Regulation
Submitted to the relevant market surveillance authority

rows.turn1_answer: Any natural or legal person may lodge a complaint, and the complaint must be submitted to the relevant market surveillance authority. The right is not limited to persons whose own rights are affected, so any grounds for considering that the Regulation has been infringed suffice. Complaints are handled in line with that authority's dedicated procedures, and the authority informs the complainant of the progress and outcome, including any judicial remedy available. Where the authority has sufficient reasons to consider that an AI system presents a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, it proceeds under Article 79 to evaluate the system and, on finding non-compliance, to require the relevant operator to take corrective action, withdraw the system from the market or recall it within a period proportionate to the risk.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)). That technical solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. The marking duty does not apply to the extent the AI system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof, or where it is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. The separate duty to disclose deep fakes, meaning AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content resembling existing persons, objects, places, entities or events that would falsely appear authentic (Article 3), falls on the deployer under Article 50(4), and any information given under Article 50 must be clear, distinguishable, accessible and provided at the latest at the time of first interaction or exposure.

criteria.criterion: Marking must be machine-readable format
Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
Solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, as far as technically feasible
Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation

rows.turn1_answer: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)). That marking solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, so far as technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards, with the AI Office facilitating codes of practice on detection and labelling of such content (Article 50(7)). The duty does not apply to the extent the AI system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof, or where the system is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. This provider-side marking duty is distinct from the deployer-side duty to disclose that deep fake image, audio or video content has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4)), and any information given to natural persons must be clear and distinguishable, provided at the latest at the time of first interaction or exposure, and conform to applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what is the scientific panel of independent experts, what are its main support/advisory tasks, and what key characteristics/selection requirements apply to its members?
rows.answer: The scientific panel is a body of independent experts that the Commission establishes by implementing act, adopted under the examination procedure of Article 98(2), to support the enforcement activities under the Regulation, with that implementing act also setting the conditions, procedures and detailed arrangements for the panel and its members to issue alerts and to request the assistance of the AI Office. Its support and advisory tasks under Article 68(3)(a) are alerting the AI Office of possible systemic risks at Union level of general-purpose AI models in accordance with the qualified alert mechanism of Article 90, contributing to the development of tools and methodologies for evaluating capabilities of general-purpose AI models and systems including through benchmarks, providing advice on the classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, providing advice on the classification of various general-purpose AI models and systems, and contributing to the development of tools and templates. Members must perform their tasks with impartiality and objectivity, must ensure the confidentiality of information and data obtained in carrying out their tasks and activities, and must neither seek nor take instructions from anyone when exercising those tasks. Each expert must draw up a declaration of interests that is made publicly available, and the AI Office must establish systems and procedures to actively manage and prevent potential conflicts of interest.

criteria.criterion: Established by Commission via implementing act (Article 98(2) examination procedure) to support enforcement, not a decision-making body itself

Tasks: advise/support AI Office on general-purpose AI models (alerting systemic risks under Article 90, developing evaluation tools/benchmarks, advising on classification); plus support market surveillance authorities, cross-border surveillance (Article 74(11)), and Union safeguard procedure (Article 81)
Selection: experts chosen by Commission for up-to-date scientific/technical AI expertise, independence from any AI provider, and ability to act diligently, accurately and objectively
Members must act impartially, confidentially and free of instructions, each publishing a declaration of interests

rows.turn1_answer: The scientific panel is a body of independent experts that the Commission establishes by implementing act, adopted under the examination procedure of Article 98(2), to support the enforcement activities under the Regulation (Article 68). Its support tasks are alerting the AI Office to possible systemic risks at Union level of general-purpose AI models through a qualified alert under Article 90, contributing to the development of tools and methodologies for evaluating the capabilities of general-purpose AI models and systems including through benchmarks, providing advice on the classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, providing advice on the classification of various general-purpose AI models and systems, and contributing to the development of tools and templates. Members must perform their tasks with impartiality and objectivity, ensure the confidentiality of information and data obtained in carrying out their tasks, and neither seek nor take instructions from anyone when exercising those tasks. Each expert must draw up a declaration of interests that is made publicly available, and the AI Office must establish systems and procedures to actively manage and prevent potential conflicts of interest, with the same implementing act laying down the conditions, procedures and detailed arrangements for the panel and its members to issue alerts and to request the assistance of the AI Office.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, if a provider identifies a serious incident during testing in real-world conditions of a high-risk AI system, what three actions must the provider take?
rows.answer: Three actions are required under Article 60(7), which governs testing of high-risk AI systems in real world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes. The provider or prospective provider must report the serious incident to the national market surveillance authority in accordance with Article 73, which requires providers to report serious incidents to the market surveillance authorities of the Member State where the incident occurred and, following that report, to carry out without delay the necessary investigations, including a risk assessment of the incident and corrective action. It must adopt immediate mitigation measures or, failing that, suspend the testing in real world conditions until such mitigation takes place, or otherwise terminate it. It must also establish a procedure for the prompt recall of the AI system upon such termination of the testing.

criteria.criterion: Perform (without delay) the necessary investigation into the incident and the AI system, including a risk assessment
Take corrective action

Cooperate with competent authorities (and notified body where relevant), and not alter the AI system in a way affecting evaluation of the incident's causes without first informing the competent authorities

rows.turn1_answer: Three actions are required. Under Article 60(7), governing testing of high-risk AI systems in real world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes, the provider or prospective provider must report any serious incident identified in the course of the testing to the national market surveillance authority in accordance with Article 73, which requires providers to report serious incidents to the market surveillance authorities of the Member State where the incident occurred within the tiered deadlines of immediately and not later than two days for a widespread infringement or a serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure, not later than 10 days in the event of the death of a person, and not later than 15 days for other serious incidents. Second, the provider must adopt immediate mitigation measures or, failing that, suspend the testing in real world conditions until such mitigation takes place, or otherwise terminate it. Third, the provider must establish a procedure for the prompt recall of the AI system upon such termination of the testing.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The Commission holds exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the Chapter V obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, taking into account the procedural guarantees of the Regulation, and it entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office, without prejudice to the Commission's powers of organisation and the division of competences between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties (Article 88). The AI Office is established within the Commission to develop Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI, with Member States facilitating the tasks entrusted to it (Article 64), and it may take the necessary actions to monitor effective compliance by providers of general-purpose AI models, including adherence to approved codes of practice, and receives duly reasoned complaints from downstream providers alleging infringement (Article 89). Market surveillance authorities may request the Commission to exercise these enforcement powers where necessary and proportionate to assist with their own tasks under the Regulation (Article 88). A scientific panel of independent experts advises and supports the AI Office, in particular by alerting it to possible systemic risks at Union level, contributing to tools and methodologies for evaluating model capabilities, and advising on the classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 68).

criteria.criterion: European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V
AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks

rows.turn1_answer: The Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the Chapter V obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94, and it entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office, without prejudice to the Commission's powers of organisation and the division of competences between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties (Article 88(1)). The AI Office is established within the Commission to develop Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI, and Member States must facilitate the tasks entrusted to it (Article 64). Market surveillance authorities may request the Commission to exercise those enforcement powers where necessary and proportionate to assist with their own tasks under the Regulation (Article 88(2)).

rows.question: What must a distributor do if it considers a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with the Act's requirements? Additionally, what extra steps are required if the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1)?
rows.answer: A distributor that considers, or has reason to consider, on the basis of the information in its possession, that a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with the requirements set out in Section 2 must not make that system available on the market until it has been brought into conformity, under Article 24(2) on distributor obligations. Where the system additionally presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the distributor must inform the provider or the importer, as applicable, to that effect. If the system has already been made available on the market, Article 24(4) requires the distributor to take the corrective actions necessary to bring it into conformity, to withdraw it or recall it, or to ensure that the provider, the importer or any relevant operator takes those actions. In that situation, where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the distributor must immediately inform the provider or importer and the authorities competent for the system concerned, giving details in particular of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken.

criteria.criterion: Not make it available on market until brought into conformity
If risk under Art 79(1): immediately inform provider or importer and the competent authorities
Notification must detail the non-compliance and any corrective actions taken

rows.turn1_answer: A distributor that considers, or has reason to consider, on the basis of the information in its possession, that a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with the requirements set out in Section 2 must, under Article 24(2), refrain from making that system available on the market until it has been brought into conformity with those requirements. Where the system has already been made available on the market, Article 24(4) requires the distributor to take the corrective actions necessary to bring it into conformity, to withdraw it or to recall it, or to ensure that the provider, the importer or any relevant operator takes those actions. If the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the distributor must in addition inform the provider or the importer of the system, as applicable, to that effect before making it available. For a system already made available on the market that presents such a risk, Article 24(4) obliges the distributor to inform immediately both the provider or importer and the authorities competent for the high-risk AI system concerned, giving details in particular of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken.

rows.question: Under Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), which categories of actors/persons does the Act apply to? List the categories.
rows.answer: Article 2(1) lists seven categories of actors. The Regulation applies to providers placing AI systems on the market or putting them into service or placing general-purpose AI models on the market in the Union irrespective of establishment, deployers of AI systems established or located within the Union, providers and deployers established or located in a third country where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union, importers and distributors of AI systems, product manufacturers placing on the market or putting into service an AI system together with their product and under their own name or trademark, authorised representatives of providers not established in the Union, and affected persons located in the Union.

criteria.criterion: Providers placing on the market/putting into service AI systems or placing on the market GPAI models in the Union
Deployers of AI systems established/located in the Union
Providers and deployers in third countries where the AI system's output is used in the Union
Importers, distributors, and product manufacturers (placing an AI system on the market/into service with their product under their own name/trademark)
Authorised representatives of providers not established in the Union
Affected persons located in the Union

rows.turn1_answer: Article 2(1) applies to seven categories of actors: providers placing AI systems on the market or putting them into service or placing general-purpose AI models on the market in the Union, whether established in the Union or in a third country, deployers of AI systems established or located in the Union, providers and deployers established or located in a third country where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union, importers and distributors of AI systems, product manufacturers placing on the market or putting into service an AI system together with their product under their own name or trademark, authorised representatives of providers not established in the Union, and affected persons located in the Union.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Only where appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented: Article 60, which permits providers or prospective providers to test high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III in real world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes, allows data collected and processed for the purpose of that testing to be transferred to third countries solely on that condition. That safeguard requirement operates alongside the other cumulative conditions in the same provision, so the transfer is lawful only while the testing itself remains compliant, including approval of the real-world testing plan by the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the testing takes place, registration of the testing with a Union-wide unique single identification number, and establishment of the provider or prospective provider in the Union or appointment of a legal representative established in the Union. Where the testing is registered in the EU database, Annex IX fixes the information to be submitted, namely the unique identification number, the name and contact details of the provider or prospective provider and of the deployers involved, a brief description of the AI system and its intended purpose, a summary of the main characteristics of the testing plan, and information on suspension or termination. Subjects of the testing may withdraw their informed consent at any time and request immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data, which constrains any onward retention or transfer of that data.

criteria.criterion: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer

rows.turn1_answer: Only where appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented, which is one of the cumulative conditions in Article 60(4) that must all be satisfied for testing of high-risk AI systems in real world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes. That condition operates alongside the other requirements in the same paragraph, notably a real-world testing plan submitted to and approved by the market surveillance authority of the Member State where the testing takes place, registration of the testing in the EU database with a Union-wide unique single identification number and the information specified in Annex IX, and establishment in the Union or appointment of an authorised representative established in the Union, which is the decisive point for a provider or prospective provider located outside the EU. Annex IX fixes that registration content as the identification number, the name and contact details of the provider or prospective provider and of the deployers involved, a brief description of the AI system and its intended purpose, a summary of the main characteristics of the testing plan, and information on suspension or termination. The Act does not itself name the specific transfer instruments, so the safeguards are those required under Union law, and subjects may at any time withdraw their informed consent and request immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data under Article 60(5).

rows.question: What are the three maximum administrative fine tiers for (a) prohibited AI practices, (b) non-compliance with obligations for high-risk AI systems and general-purpose AI (GPAI) models, and (c) supplying incorrect/incomplete/misleading information? For each tier, give the maximum amount in EUR and the alternative maximum as a percentage of worldwide annual turnover.
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibited practices carries the highest ceiling, up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, under Article 99(3). The middle tier is up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, applying under Article 99(4) to the closed list of operator and notified body duties covering provider obligations under Article 16, authorised representative obligations under Article 22, importer obligations under Article 23, distributor obligations under Article 24, deployer obligations under Article 26, notified body requirements under Articles 31, 33(1), (3) and (4) and 34, and the transparency obligations under Article 50, and mirrored for general-purpose AI model providers by Article 101, under which the Commission may fine a provider up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of annual total worldwide turnover, whichever is higher, for infringing the relevant provisions, for failing to comply with an information request or supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, for failing to comply with a requested measure, or for refusing model access for evaluation. The lowest tier is up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, under Article 99(5) for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities in reply to a request. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) inverts the comparison so that each of those ceilings is the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount.

criteria.criterion: Prohibited AI practices (Article 5): up to EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever higher
High-risk/GPAI obligations (Articles 16, 22, 23, 24, 26, 31, 33(1)(3)(4), 34, 50): up to EUR 15,000,000 or 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever higher
Incorrect/incomplete/misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities: up to EUR 7,500,000 or 1% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever higher

rows.turn1_answer: Article 99 sets three ceilings, each applied as whichever of the fixed amount or the turnover percentage is higher. Non-compliance with the prohibited AI practices in Article 5, which bans practices such as manipulative techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring and real-time remote biometric identification by law enforcement, attracts up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year under Article 99(3). Non-compliance by operators and notified bodies with the closed list in Article 99(4), covering provider obligations under Article 16, authorised representative obligations under Article 22, importer obligations under Article 23, distributor obligations under Article 24, deployer obligations under Article 26, notified body requirements under Articles 31, 33(1), (3) and (4) and 34, and the transparency obligations under Article 50, attracts up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 %, and the supply of incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities attracts up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % under Article 99(5), with Article 99(6) applying the lower of the two figures to SMEs including start-ups. Providers of general-purpose AI models are fined separately by the Commission under Article 101 at up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of annual total worldwide turnover, whichever is higher, for intentional or negligent infringements of the relevant provisions, failure to supply requested documents or information or supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, failure to comply with a requested measure, or failure to grant model access for evaluation.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what is the EU database for high-risk AI systems, what categories of information must it contain, and who is the controller of that database?
rows.answer: The EU database is a single Union-level registry that the Commission sets up and maintains in collaboration with the Member States under Article 71, covering high-risk AI systems registered under Article 49, systems classified as not high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation, and real-world testing registered under Article 60, with the data held in a publicly accessible part and, for the Annex III areas of biometrics, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, in a secure non-public section to which only the Commission and the national authorities designated under Article 74(8) have access. Its content is the information listed in Sections A and B of Annex VIII, entered by the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative, covering provider identification and contact details, system identification, intended purpose and status, plus the Annex IX information for testing in real world conditions, and it holds personal data only so far as necessary, namely the names and contact details of the natural persons responsible for registering the system who have legal authority to represent the provider or the deployer. Registration in the database is a precondition under Article 49 for placing an Annex III high-risk AI system on the market or putting it into service, and failure to register is formal non-compliance under Article 83, which the market surveillance authority must require to be rectified and, if it persists, escalate to restriction, recall or withdrawal. As to control, the Commission is the controller of the EU database, and the Act attributes to it responsibility for the database and for providing adequate technical and administrative support to the entering parties.

criteria.criterion: EU database (set up/maintained by Commission with Member States) covers high-risk AI systems under Art 6(2) registered per Arts 49 and 60, and non-high-risk Art 6(3) systems registered per Art 6(4) and 49
Categories: Annex VIII Sections A and B entered by provider/authorised representative; Section C entered by deployer that is/acts on behalf of a public authority, agency or body
Controller: the Commission

rows.turn1_answer: The EU database for high-risk AI systems is the Union-level registration database that the Commission sets up and maintains in collaboration with the Member States under Article 71, covering high-risk AI systems under Article 6(2) registered under Article 49, systems classified as not high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation, and testing in real world conditions registered under Article 60. It must contain the information listed in Sections A and B of Annex VIII, entered by the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative, and it may contain personal data only in so far as necessary, namely the names and contact details of the natural persons responsible for registering the system who have legal authority to represent the provider or the deployer. For high-risk AI systems in the areas of law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management listed in points 1, 6 and 7 of Annex III, registration takes place in a secure non-public section accessible only to the Commission and the national authorities referred to in Article 74(8), with a reduced set of Annex VIII and Annex IX information. The Commission is the controller of the database, having established and maintaining it and consulting relevant experts on its functional specifications and the Board on their updating.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the two conditions are alternatives rather than cumulative. Article 51(1) classifies a general-purpose AI model as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it meets any of the following conditions: it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks, or, based on a decision of the Commission taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those, having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII. Under Article 51(2) high impact capabilities are presumed where the cumulative amount of computation used for training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10^25, and Article 51(3) empowers the Commission to amend those thresholds and supplement the benchmarks and indicators by delegated act. Where the model meets the Article 51(1)(a) condition the provider must notify the Commission within two weeks under Article 52(1), and may present sufficiently substantiated arguments under Article 52(2) that the model exceptionally does not present systemic risks due to its specific characteristics.

criteria.criterion: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices

rows.turn1_answer: No, the two conditions are alternatives rather than cumulative. Under Article 51, which sets the classification rule for general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, a model falls into that category either where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks, or where the Commission decides, on its own initiative or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, that the model has capabilities or impact equivalent to those, having regard to the designation criteria listed in Annex XIII. For the first limb, a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10^25, a threshold the Commission may amend to reflect technological developments. Classification as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk adds the Article 55 obligations on top of the Article 53 duties, including model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools with adversarial testing.

rows.question: For a high-risk AI system, who is responsible for ensuring that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the system's intended purpose, and under what condition does that responsibility apply?
rows.answer: The provider bears this responsibility, and it applies only where the high-risk AI system is developed using techniques involving the training of AI models with data. Article 10 requires that training, validation and testing data sets be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose, and Article 10(3) requires those data sets to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. Under Article 42(1), high-risk AI systems trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting in which they are intended to be used are presumed to comply with the relevant data governance requirements. The provider must also communicate this downstream, since Article 13 requires the instructions for use to state, when appropriate, specifications for the input data and other relevant information on the training, validation and testing data sets used, taking into account the intended purpose.

criteria.criterion: Provider of the high-risk AI system
Applies whenever the system is developed using techniques involving training AI models with data (Art. 10(1))
For systems not using such training techniques, applies only to testing data sets (Art. 10(6))

rows.turn1_answer: The deployer bears that responsibility, and it applies only to the extent the deployer exercises control over the input data. Article 26, which requires deployers to use a high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions for use, to assign human oversight to competent and trained natural persons, and to monitor its operation, confines this input data duty to data within the deployer's control and measures it against the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system. The parallel obligation on the provider is distinct: Article 10 requires training, validation and testing data sets to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, under data governance practices appropriate to that purpose.

rows.question: I am a distributor of an AI systems. Do I have obligation not to jeopardize its conformity? I was not told if the system is high-risk or not. What if am I am importer instead?
rows.answer: Yes. Article 24(3) requires distributors to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise the system's compliance with the requirements of Section 2, and Article 24(1) requires them to verify, before making it available on the market, that it bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the instructions for use. These duties attach only where the system is high-risk, so that classification must be established first, and under Article 24(2) a distributor that considers or has reason to consider the system non-conforming must not make it available until it has been brought into conformity, and must inform the provider or the importer where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1). An importer bears a corresponding duty under Article 23, which requires importers to verify before placing a high-risk AI system on the market that the conformity assessment, technical documentation, CE marking and accompanying documents are in order, and to ensure that storage and transport conditions under their responsibility do not jeopardise the system's compliance with those same requirements.

criteria.criterion: Yes, obligation applies regardless of high-risk knowledge
Distributor: storage/transport must not jeopardise Section 2 compliance (Article 24(3))
Importer: same obligation applies (Article 23(4))

rows.turn1_answer: Yes. Article 24(3) requires a distributor to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under its responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the system's compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2, and this duty is triggered only where the system is high-risk, so it applies on the stated high-risk classification and not to systems outside that tier. Article 24(2) reinforces this by prohibiting a distributor from making the system available on the market where it considers, or has reason to consider on the basis of the information in its possession, that the system is not in conformity with those requirements, and by requiring it to inform the provider or the importer where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1). An importer is subject to the equivalent duty under Article 23(3), which requires importers to ensure that storage or transport conditions, while the high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, do not jeopardise its compliance with the same requirements, and a distributor must in any event verify under Article 24(1) that the importer has complied with that obligation.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: Not automatically high-risk. Article 6(1) makes a safety component high-risk only where both conditions hold, namely that the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, and that the product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment for its placing on the market under that legislation. A Class I device that is non-sterile, has no measuring function and is not a reusable surgical instrument is self-assessed by the manufacturer without notified body involvement, so the second condition is not met and the Annex I route does not apply. The system would still be high-risk if the intended purpose falls within a use case listed in Annex III under Article 6(2), and any reclassification of the device into a higher class requiring a notified body would bring it back within Article 6(1).

criteria.criterion: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply

rows.turn1_answer: No, not automatically. Article 6(1) makes an AI system high-risk only where two cumulative conditions are met: it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. A non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable-surgical Class I device is self-certified by the manufacturer without notified body involvement, so the second condition fails and the Annex I route does not classify the system as high-risk. It could still become high-risk under Article 6(2) if it independently falls within one of the listed Annex III use cases, subject to the Article 6(3) derogation for systems posing no significant risk of harm that perform a narrow procedural task, improve the result of a previously completed human activity, detect decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment, or perform a preparatory task, which never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), can the same AI system be subject both to the Act's "high-risk AI system" obligations and to the transparency obligations sometimes described informally as "limited risk"? Explain briefly.
rows.answer: Yes, the same AI system can carry both sets of duties, because they are cumulative rather than alternative. Article 50(6) expressly provides that the transparency obligations in Article 50(1) to (4) do not affect the requirements and obligations set out in Chapter III, so classification as high-risk does not displace them, and they operate without prejudice to other transparency obligations under Union or national law. The Article 50 duties attach to the functional characteristics of the system and to the actor concerned, namely a provider whose system interacts directly with natural persons (Article 50(1)) or generates synthetic audio, image, video or text content that must be marked in a machine-readable and detectable format (Article 50(2)), and a deployer operating an emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system who must inform the persons exposed (Article 50(3)) or generating deep fake content who must disclose that it is artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4)), subject in each case to the stated derogations such as law-enforcement authorisation. The informal label "limited risk" describes no separate tier that excludes high-risk status, and Article 79(6) confirms the overlap by treating a failure to meet the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements and non-compliance with Article 50 as distinct grounds on which market surveillance authorities may act against the same system.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Article 50(6): Article 50(1)-(4) transparency duties do not affect Chapter III high-risk obligations
Obligations are cumulative, not mutually exclusive

rows.turn1_answer: Yes, the two sets of obligations apply cumulatively to the same system. Article 13 requires a high-risk AI system to be designed so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, and to be accompanied by instructions for use covering the provider's identity, the intended purpose, the level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, human oversight measures and, when appropriate, specifications for the input data. That duty runs to the deployer and does not displace the separate transparency duties owed to the natural persons exposed to the system, which is why Article 26(11) expressly preserves the Article 50 information obligations towards end users where the high-risk system is an Annex III biometric identification, emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system.
