The informal "limited risk" label therefore describes a layer of transparency duties, not a mutually exclusive tier, so a system that is high-risk under Article 6 carries the Chapter III requirements and any applicable Article 50 transparency obligations at the same time.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a toy qualify as a high-risk AI system, and if so under what conditions?
rows.answer: An AI system intended to be used as a toy is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a toy covered by Directive 2009/48/EC on the safety of toys, which is listed in and that toy is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment before being placed on the market or put into service, both conditions being cumulative under Article 6(1). Where the toy manufacturer may instead self-assess conformity under the toy safety legislation, the second condition of Article 6(1) is not met and the AI system is not high-risk on that route, unless it independently falls within an Annex III use case under Article 6(2). This classification applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the toy. Where it is high-risk, the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required under Directive 2009/48/EC pursuant to Article 43, with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Condition: AI system is a toy or safety component of a toy covered by Directive 2009/48/EC (Annex I harmonisation legislation)
Condition: that toy is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Directive
Both conditions cumulative (Article 6(1))

rows.turn1_answer: An AI system intended to be used as a toy is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a toy covered by Directive 2009/48/EC on the safety of toys, which is listed in Annex I, and that toy is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment before being placed on the market or put into service, both conditions being cumulative under Article 6(1). Where the toy manufacturer may instead rely on internal production control because harmonised standards covering all relevant safety requirements have been applied, the second condition of Article 6(1) is not met and the system is not high-risk on that route. Classification under Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the toy. Where the system does qualify, the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required under Directive 2009/48/EC pursuant to Article 43(3), with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a lift is high-risk where both conditions in Article 6(1) are met: it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes, at point 4, Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts and safety components for lifts, and that lift or safety component is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that Directive. This classification applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift. Where it is high-risk on this basis, the provider follows, under Article 43, the conformity assessment procedure required by Directive 2014/33/EU itself, with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 forming part of that assessment, and a new conformity assessment is required in the event of a substantial modification.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative

rows.turn1_answer: An AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift is high-risk where both conditions in Article 6(1) are met: it is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes, at point 4, Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts and safety components for lifts, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that Directive. This applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift. Where the classification is established, the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required under Directive 2014/33/EU pursuant to Article 43(3), with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 forming part of that assessment, and a new conformity assessment is required in the event of a substantial modification under Article 43(4).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), are AI systems intended for emotion recognition from biometric data always prohibited? If not, in which contexts are they prohibited, what exception applies, and how are they classified when not prohibited?
rows.answer: Emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited under the AI Act; the prohibition in Article 5 only applies in workplaces and educational institutions, with a narrow medical/safety exception. Elsewhere the system is high-risk under Annex III.1(c) and triggers Article 50(3) transparency duties toward exposed persons.

criteria.criterion: No
Prohibited context: inferring emotions of natural persons in workplace and education institutions (Article 5(1)(f))
Exception: use intended for medical or safety reasons
When not prohibited, classified as high-risk under Annex III (emotion recognition/biometrics category)

rows.turn1_answer: Emotion recognition is not categorically prohibited under the AI Act; the prohibition in Article 5 only applies in workplaces and educational institutions, with a narrow medical/safety exception. Elsewhere the system is high-risk under Annex III.1(c) and triggers Article 50(3) transparency duties toward exposed persons.

rows.question: I generated audio with AI for my artistic work (sole purpose). Do I need to provide some marking of its artificial nature? I feel that would compromise the enjoyment of the work.
rows.answer: Yes, some marking is required, but the artistic character of the work shapes only part of it. Where the audio constitutes a deep fake, the deployer duty in Article 50(4) to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated is limited, for content forming part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work, to disclosure of the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work, so a credit, programme note or accompanying metadata suffices rather than an intrusive on-work label. The separate provider duty in Article 50(2) is not relaxed by artistic purpose: providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, by solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, and this applies unless the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics, or the use is authorised by law for criminal-offence purposes. Under Article 50(5) that information must reach the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of first exposure and must conform to applicable accessibility requirements.

criteria.criterion: Yes, disclosure still required
No need for marking that hampers enjoyment
Must disclose existence of AI-generated content in appropriate/unobtrusive manner

rows.turn1_answer: Yes, some disclosure remains required, though the artistic character of the work limits its form rather than removing the duty. Where the AI-generated audio constitutes a deep fake, Article 50(4) obliges the deployer to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, but where that content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work, the third subparagraph of Article 50(4) limits the obligation to disclosing the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work, so a placement such as credits or accompanying notice suffices rather than an intrusive overlay. That artistic limitation does not extend to Article 50(2), under which the provider of the generative AI system must ensure the synthetic audio output is marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, that marking being technical and imperceptible in performance. The only exemptions from the deep fake disclosure duty are use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, which does not arise here.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: The combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm.

criteria.criterion: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm

rows.turn1_answer: The combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm.

rows.question: For AI systems that fit within the use cases listed in Annex III but are considered non-high-risk by the provider, do they need to be registered in the EU database?
rows.answer: Yes, registration is still required. Article 6(3) allows a provider to conclude that an Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, unless it profiles natural persons, and Article 6(4) requires that assessment to be documented before the system is placed on the market and expressly makes the provider subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2). Under Article 49(2), the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative must register itself and that system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 before placing it on the market or putting it into service, with the Article 6(3) non-high-risk information entered in Section B of Annex VIII.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Registration required under Article 49(2)
Registered in EU database referred to in Article 71

rows.turn1_answer: Yes. A provider that concludes under the Article 6(3) derogation that an Annex III system is not high-risk must document that assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and remains subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2). Article 49(2) requires that provider, or where applicable the authorised representative, to register themselves and that system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service. The Article 71 database, set up and maintained by the Commission, expressly covers both high-risk AI systems and AI systems that are not considered high-risk pursuant to Article 6(3), and the provider or authorised representative enters the Annex VIII information, Section B of which is dedicated to those Article 6(3) non-high-risk assessments.

rows.question: Do I need informed consent to test a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside a regulatory sandbox?
rows.answer: Yes. Testing high-risk AI systems in real world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes under Article 60 requires freely-given informed consent from the subjects of testing, obtained prior to their participation and after they have been duly informed in concise, clear, relevant and understandable terms about the nature and objectives of the testing and possible inconvenience, the conditions and expected duration of participation, their rights including the right to refuse and to withdraw at any time without detriment or justification, the arrangements for requesting reversal or disregarding of the system's predictions, recommendations or decisions, and the Union-wide unique single identification number of the testing together with the contact details of the provider or its legal representative (Article 61(1)). That consent must be dated and documented, and a copy given to the subject of testing or their legal representative (Article 61(2)). Subjects may withdraw at any time by revoking their informed consent and may request immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data, without this affecting activities already carried out (Article 60(5)). Consent does not stand alone: the provider or prospective provider must also draw up a real-world testing plan, submit it to and obtain approval from the market surveillance authority in the Member State concerned, and register the testing as required, before testing may begin (Article 60(4)).

criteria.criterion: Yes

Consent must be freely given and informed, obtained prior to participation, covering nature/objectives/inconveniences, conditions and duration, rights to refuse/withdraw without detriment or justification, reversal/disregard arrangements, and the unique ID plus provider contact details
Consent must be dated, documented, and a copy given to the subject or their legal representative

rows.turn1_answer: Yes. Testing a high-risk AI system in real world conditions outside an AI regulatory sandbox requires freely-given informed consent from the subjects of testing, obtained prior to their participation and after they have been given concise, clear, relevant and understandable information on the nature and objectives of the testing and any inconvenience linked to participation, the conditions and expected duration of participation, their right to refuse and to withdraw at any time without detriment or justification, the arrangements for requesting reversal or disregarding of the system's predictions, recommendations or decisions, and the Union-wide unique single identification number of the testing together with the contact details of the provider or its legal representative (Article 61(1)). That consent must be dated and documented, with a copy given to the subject of testing or their legal representative (Article 61(2)), and withdrawal of consent, which may be accompanied by a request for immediate and permanent deletion of personal data, does not affect activities already carried out (Article 60(5)). Consent alone is not sufficient: under Article 60(4) the provider or prospective provider may test only where a real-world testing plan has been drawn up and submitted to the market surveillance authority of the Member State concerned, that authority has approved the testing and the plan (approval being tacit after 30 days unless national law requires express authorisation), the testing has been registered with a Union-wide unique single identification number, and the provider is established in the Union or has appointed a legal representative established in the Union.

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Both, and the duties run in parallel rather than sequentially. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring it into conformity, withdraw it, disable it, or recall it, and must inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and importers. Under Article 20(2), where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), meaning a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the certificate, of the nature of the non-compliance and of any corrective action taken. The market surveillance authority's own evaluation under Article 79(2) is a separate enforcement track that can require corrective action within a prescribed period, and it does not displace or postpone the provider's immediate obligations, since the operator must in any event cooperate with the authority and ensure appropriate corrective action for all affected systems made available on the Union market.

criteria.criterion: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority

rows.turn1_answer: Both, and they are cumulative rather than alternative. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring it into conformity, withdraw it, disable it, or recall it, and inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and importers. Under Article 20(2), where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), meaning a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, and the provider becomes aware of that risk, the provider must immediately investigate the causes in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the certificate, of the nature of the non-compliance and of any corrective action taken. The market surveillance authority's own evaluation under Article 79(2), which may require the operator to bring the system into compliance, withdraw it or recall it, is a separate and additional track that does not suspend or postpone the provider's immediate duties, and the operator must cooperate with that authority and ensure appropriate corrective action is taken for all systems concerned.

rows.question: What is Article 50(4) about?
rows.answer: Article 50(4) imposes the deepfake disclosure duty on deployers: anyone deploying an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, unless the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, the duty is limited to disclosing the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. The same paragraph adds a separate duty for deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, who must disclose that the text was artificially generated or manipulated. That text duty alone falls away where the use is authorised by law for criminal law purposes or where the content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for its publication, and this editorial exemption does not excuse the deepfake disclosure.

criteria.criterion: Deployers of AI systems generating/manipulating image, audio or video constituting a deep fake must disclose the content is artificially generated or manipulated
Exception where use is authorised by law to detect/prevent/investigate/prosecute criminal offences
For evidently artistic/creative/satirical/fictional/analogous works, obligation limited to disclosing existence of such content without hampering enjoyment/display

Separate rule: deployers of AI systems generating/manipulating text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose artificial generation, with exceptions for law-enforcement authorisation or human review/editorial responsibility

rows.turn1_answer: Article 50(4) imposes the deployer-side transparency duties for artificially generated or manipulated content. Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, save that where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional work the disclosure is limited to an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must likewise disclose that the text was artificially generated or manipulated, unless the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, or the content has undergone human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for its publication. That editorial-review exemption applies only to the text duty and does not excuse the deep fake disclosure, which sits alongside the provider duties in Article 50 to inform natural persons that they are interacting with an AI system and to mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format.

rows.question: Is an AI system high-risk if it is used in a product that: is not listed in Annex I; use case not listed in Annex III; internally uses general purpose AI model with systemic risk due to high impact capabilities?
rows.answer: Not high-risk. Under Article 6, an AI system is high-risk only on two routes: where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, or where it serves one of the Annex III use cases spanning biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, and justice; neither route is met here, and the system does not fall within the prohibited practices of Article 5. The fact that the system internally relies on a general-purpose AI model classified as presenting systemic risk on account of high impact capabilities does not alter the classification of the AI system, since the systemic-risk qualification attaches to the model and its provider, not to the downstream AI system. The system therefore remains outside the high-risk tier, subject only to the Article 50 transparency obligations where it interacts directly with natural persons or generates synthetic audio, image, video or text content that must be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.

criteria.criterion: No
Article 6(1) not met: not an Annex I product/safety component requiring third-party conformity assessment
Article 6(2) not met: use case not listed in Annex III
Internal use of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk is not an Article 6 criterion

rows.turn1_answer: Not high-risk. Under Article 6, an AI system is high-risk only on two routes: where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, or where it serves one of the use cases in the eight areas of Annex III; a system meeting neither route falls outside the high-risk tier. The fact that the system internally relies on a general-purpose AI model classified as presenting systemic risk on account of high impact capabilities does not alter that classification, because systemic-risk status attaches obligations to the provider of that model and is not a route to high-risk classification for the downstream system under Article 6. Where the system interacts directly with natural persons or generates synthetic audio, image, video or text content, the provider remains subject to the transparency obligations of Article 50, including marking outputs in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, save where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing, does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics, or is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The model did not hallucinate. Article 24(3) expressly requires distributors to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the system's compliance with the requirements of Section 2, and the words "where applicable" accommodate the fact that some high-risk AI systems are supplied as or within physical products, on hardware or on storage media whose integrity can be affected by handling, temperature, humidity or tampering. Where a distributor considers, or has reason to consider, on the basis of the information in its possession, that a system it has already made available on the market no longer conforms to those requirements, Article 24(4) requires it to take the necessary corrective actions to bring the system into conformity, to withdraw or recall it, or to ensure the provider, importer or other relevant operator does so, and where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) to inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities immediately, with details of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken.

criteria.criterion: No, not hallucinated
Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)

rows.turn1_answer: The local model was correct, not hallucinating. Article 24(3) requires distributors to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the system's compliance with the Section 2 requirements, and the qualifier "where applicable" is what accommodates systems supplied purely as software. The duty is real because a high-risk AI system may be shipped as a physical product or as a safety component of one, or on physical media whose handling can affect conformity. Alongside it, Article 24(1) obliges the distributor, before making the system available on the market, to verify the CE marking and the accompanying EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use, and Article 24(4) obliges corrective action, withdrawal or recall where the distributor has reason to consider a system already made available is not in conformity.

rows.question:
Given an AI system that is high-risk according to Annex III: if it is repurposed to a use case not in Annex III (nor Annex I), then:
- the repurposed AI system is still high-risk due to reversibility of training into the original system
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk but it must be reported in the EU database
- the repurposed AI system is no longer high-risk and there is no need to report it in the EU database
rows.answer: No longer high-risk, and no entry in the EU database is required. Classification under Article 6(2) turns on the intended purpose falling within one of the lettered use cases under the eight Annex III areas, so a system whose intended purpose lies outside Annex III and which is not a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation subject to third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), is outside the high-risk tier; reversibility of training or the system's earlier classification is not a criterion. The EU database maintained by the Commission under Article 71 covers only high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2) registered in accordance with Articles 49 and 60, together with systems not considered high-risk pursuant to the Article 6(3) derogation and registered under Article 6(4) and Article 49, and a system falling entirely outside Annex III belongs to neither group. Note that the Article 6(3) derogation, which excludes an Annex III system posing no significant risk of harm because it performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, and which never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, is the only route that does carry a registration duty despite the non-high-risk outcome.

criteria.criterion: No longer high-risk (third option)
High-risk status attaches to intended purpose/use case under Article 6(2)/Annex III, not to the system or its training as such
New use case outside Annex III and Annex I means neither limb of Article 6 is satisfied
No registration/EU database obligation (Article 49/Article 71) since system is not high-risk

rows.turn1_answer: The third option is correct: the repurposed system is no longer high-risk and needs no entry in the EU database. Classification under Article 6(2) turns on the intended purpose of the system as placed on the market, so a system whose intended purpose no longer corresponds to any lettered use case under the eight Annex III areas, and which is not a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), falls outside the high-risk tier entirely; prior training for a high-risk purpose is not a classification criterion. Registration duties in Article 71(1) reach only high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2) registered under Articles 49 and 60, together with systems escaping high-risk status by the Article 6(3) derogation and registered under Article 6(4) and Article 49, and a system outside Annex III altogether belongs to neither group. The change of intended purpose is itself a substantial matter for the provider to document, and if the system were later returned to an Annex III use case the full high-risk regime, including registration, would again apply.

rows.question: We have a phone system where the caller can press 1 if they consent to the call being recorded, 2 if they do not. We wish to replace this with an NLP system that understands a voice reply like "Yes", "Sure", "Please no", etc. Would such a system be considered high-risk? It's for our clinic.
rows.answer: Not high-risk. Recognising a spoken affirmative or negative reply to a recording-consent prompt falls outside both routes of Article 6: the system is neither a product nor a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and subject to third-party conformity assessment, and it is not one of the lettered use cases under the eight areas of Annex III, whose essential private and public services area reaches only matters such as evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services including healthcare services, and the evaluation and classification of emergency calls, dispatch priority, and emergency healthcare patient triage. Even on the most expansive reading of the clinic setting, the Article 6(3) derogation would remove the system from the high-risk tier, because interpreting a yes or no answer is a narrow procedural task that poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making, provided the system performs no profiling of natural persons, which would always make it high-risk. The system therefore sits in the minimal risk tier under the Regulation, and consent to recording remains governed by data protection law rather than by the high-risk requirements.

criteria.criterion: No
Not biometric categorisation or emotion recognition under Annex III(1)(b)-(c), since the system parses semantic content (yes/no), not emotional or protected-attribute inference
Not essential healthcare services under Annex III(5)(a), since consent capture for call recording is not an eligibility evaluation for benefits/services

rows.turn1_answer: Not high-risk. Capturing a spoken "yes" or "no" to a recording-consent prompt is neither a safety component of, nor itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)), nor does it match any lettered use case in Annex III (Article 6(2)); in the healthcare-adjacent area of access to essential private and public services, Annex III reaches only evaluation of eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services including healthcare by or on behalf of public authorities, creditworthiness or credit scoring, risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance, and the evaluation and classification of emergency calls or the dispatching and prioritisation of emergency first response services including emergency healthcare patient triage, none of which a consent-capture function performs. If the intended purpose were later extended, for example to assess or prioritise callers rather than simply register a consent reply, that reclassification would have to be reassessed under Article 6, and whoever modifies the intended purpose so that the system becomes high-risk is itself considered the provider under Article 25(1).

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: Drones are neither prohibited nor high-risk as such, classification follows the AI function, not the airframe. Using AI in a drone to identify who is present around a town is a prohibited practice under Article 5(1)(h) where it constitutes real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, which is permitted only for the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation and the search for missing persons, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons or of a terrorist attack, and the localisation or identification of a person suspected of an Annex II offence punishable by at least four years' custodial sentence; outside law enforcement use that prohibition does not bite, and Article 5 also bans, among the other listed practices, biometric categorisation deducing race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, and criminal-offence risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits. That prohibition attaches to the practice regardless of whether the carrier is a toy drone. For toy drones in other applications, the AI is high-risk under Article 6(1) only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Directive 2009/48/EC on the safety of toys as listed in Annex I and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment; failing that, the use is minimal risk, subject only to the Article 50 obligation on providers to ensure that persons interacting directly with the AI system are informed of that fact unless it is obvious.

criteria.criterion: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)

rows.turn1_answer: Drones are not as such a prohibited or high-risk category: the tier follows the AI function performed, not the airframe. Deploying a drone-mounted AI system to identify who is present in a town amounts to the use of a 'real-time' remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces, which Article 5 prohibits only where used for the purposes of law enforcement, and then subject to the strictly necessary exceptions of targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation and search for missing persons, prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable terrorist attack, and localisation or identification of a suspect for an Annex II offence punishable by at least four years' custodial sentence; outside law enforcement that use is not among the practices prohibited by Article 5, although Article 5 does separately prohibit biometric categorisation deducing race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, whoever operates the drone. A toy drone is high-risk only where Article 6(1) is satisfied, that is where the AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Directive 2009/48/EC on the safety of toys listed in Annex I and that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment for placing on the market; a toy drone put to other applications is assessed the same way, so that if it falls outside the Annex I toy safety route and outside the Annex III use cases it is not high-risk. In either case, where such a system is intended to interact directly with natural persons, Article 50 requires the provider to ensure those persons are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious in the circumstances and context of use.

rows.question: Does the EU AI Act establish a "proportionality of need" requirement according to which very powerful but environmentally impactful models (e.g. LLMs) should not be used for simple tasks (e.g. sentiment recognition) when a simpler and performant model is available (e.g. BERT)? If yes, cite which Article or Annex mentions this.
rows.answer: No. No Article or Annex of the EU AI Act imposes a "proportionality of need" duty to select a smaller or less energy-intensive model for a simpler task, and model choice as such is not regulated: environmental protection appears only as a protected interest in the statement of purpose in Article 1(1), which frames the Regulation's harmonised rules, prohibitions, high-risk requirements, transparency rules and general-purpose AI model rules, not as an operative obligation on providers or deployers. The closest the Regulation comes is Article 112(6), under which the Commission must report by 2 August 2028 and every four years thereafter on progress in developing standardisation deliverables on the energy-efficient development of general-purpose AI models and assess the need for further measures, including binding ones, which confirms that no binding energy-efficiency or model-right-sizing requirement exists yet. For general-purpose AI models the only related duties are documentary, namely the Article 53(1) obligations to draw up and keep up to date technical documentation of the model including its training and testing process and evaluation results per Annex XI, to make integration information available to downstream providers per Annex XII, to put in place a copyright policy, and to publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the training content. Where the model meets the Article 51 systemic-risk threshold, the additional Article 55 obligations on evaluation, systemic-risk mitigation, serious-incident reporting and cybersecurity apply, but none of these turns on whether a lighter model could have performed the task.

criteria.criterion: No
No provision conditions use of a capable model on unavailability of a simpler/less resource-intensive alternative for the same task
Obligations are risk- and capability-based (e.g. Article 6, Annex III, Article 51), not tied to model right-sizing or environmental impact

rows.turn1_answer: No. Neither an Article nor an Annex establishes a "proportionality of need" requirement obliging a provider or deployer to choose the least powerful or least energy-intensive model capable of performing a given task, so using a general-purpose AI model for a simple task is not as such a breach. Environmental protection features only as a general objective in Article 1(1), which frames the Regulation as promoting human-centric and trustworthy AI while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights including environmental protection, and that objective creates no model-selection duty. The single operative environmental provision is Article 112(6), which requires the Commission to report by 2 August 2028 and every four years thereafter on progress on standardisation deliverables on the energy-efficient development of general-purpose AI models and to assess the need for further measures or actions, including binding ones. Energy efficiency is therefore currently addressed through future standardisation and review rather than through any binding proportionality obligation on operators.

rows.question: Article 9 of the AI Act lists the five categories of harm that map to AI systems with: no risk, limited risk, high-risk, systemic risk, prohibited. What are the five categories and how do they map to the five risk levels?
rows.answer: No such mapping exists in Article 9. Article 9 does not enumerate categories of harm or risk levels at all: it requires a risk management system to be established, implemented, documented and maintained for high-risk AI systems, covering identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks, estimation of risks arising in intended use and under reasonably foreseeable misuse, testing against pre-defined metrics, and residual risks judged acceptable and communicated to the deployer, and the interests it protects are three rather than five, namely health, safety and fundamental rights. The tiers referred to are established by separate provisions: Article 5 prohibits eight practices, being subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, social scoring by any public or private provider or deployer, criminal-risk profiling based solely on personality traits, untargeted scraping of facial images for facial recognition databases, emotion recognition in workplaces and education institutions, biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, subject in the last case to the three exhaustive objectives in Article 5(1)(h) with prior judicial or administrative authorisation. Systemic risk is not a system-level tier but a classification of general-purpose AI models under Article 51, arising from high-impact capabilities, presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations, or by Commission decision on the Annex XIII criteria of parameters, data, compute, modalities, benchmarks and reach, and it triggers the Article 55 duties of model evaluation including adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting, and cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. The Act attaches no obligations to systems described as carrying no risk, and the transparency duties often labelled limited risk are not part of Article 9.

criteria.criterion: No
Article 9 only establishes the risk management system for high-risk AI systems, not a five-tier harm classification

Four steps: identify/analyze risks (9(2)(a)); estimate/evaluate risks under intended use and foreseeable misuse (9(2)(b)); evaluate risks from post-market monitoring data (9(2)(c)); adopt targeted risk management measures (9(2)(d))
The prohibited/high-risk/limited-risk/minimal-risk/systemic-risk tiering comes from elsewhere in the Regulation (e.g. Articles 5, 6, 50, 51), not Article 9

rows.turn1_answer: No such taxonomy exists: Article 9 does not enumerate five categories of harm, and it does not map anything to risk levels. Article 9 requires a risk management system established, implemented, documented and maintained for high-risk AI systems, under which the provider identifies and analyses the known and reasonably foreseeable risks the system can pose to three protected interests only, namely health, safety or fundamental rights, estimates and evaluates the risks arising in intended use and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, tests the system to select targeted risk management measures, and judges the residual risks acceptable and communicates them to the deployer. The tiers themselves sit elsewhere: the prohibited tier is fixed by Article 5, which bans eight practices, namely subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques materially distorting behaviour and causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, social scoring by any provider or deployer whether public or private leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or disproportionate to the social behaviour, criminal-risk profiling based solely on personality traits, untargeted scraping of facial images to build facial recognition databases, emotion recognition in workplaces and educational institutions save for medical or safety reasons, biometric categorisation inferring race, ethnicity, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, sex life or sexual orientation apart from lawful labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric data sets, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes subject to the three exhaustively listed objectives with prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation. Systemic risk is a separate concept applying only to general-purpose AI models under Article 51, presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations or where the Commission so designates the model on the Annex XIII criteria, and the Act contains no operative tier labelled "no risk" or "limited risk".

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No. Deployers of a high-risk AI system must use it in accordance with the instructions for use, which under Article 13 must state the intended purpose and the known or foreseeable circumstances, including reasonably foreseeable misuse, that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, so a use outside the intended purpose is not made permissible by an internal conclusion that the new use is itself low-risk. Under Article 25(1), a deployer that modifies the intended purpose of a high-risk AI system already placed on the market is considered a provider of that system and assumes the full provider obligations, with Article 25(2) requiring the initial provider to make available the information, technical access and assistance needed to meet them, in particular for the conformity assessment. Logging remains mandatory: Article 26(6) requires the deployer to keep the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system, to the extent those logs are under its control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the system and in any event at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law, in particular Union data protection law, provides otherwise. Deployers that are financial institutions subject to internal governance requirements under Union financial services law satisfy that retention duty by maintaining the logs as part of the documentation kept under that law.

criteria.criterion: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use

rows.turn1_answer: No, the new use cannot simply be adopted. A deployer must use a high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying it (Article 26), and those instructions state the intended purpose and the known or foreseeable circumstances of reasonably foreseeable misuse that may lead to risks (Article 13(3)); operating outside that intended purpose is a breach of Article 26 irrespective of the legal team's own risk view, and under Article 25 a deployer that modifies the intended purpose of a high-risk AI system already placed on the market is itself considered a provider and assumes the full provider obligations. That the new use is not caught by Annex I or Annex III does not neutralise this, because the system deployed remains the same high-risk AI system and the deployer's classification-based reasoning does not displace the instructions for use. Logs must therefore still be kept: the deployer retains the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system, to the extent they are under its control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and in any event at least six months, unless Union or national law, in particular Union data protection law, provides otherwise, with deployers that are financial institutions subject to Union financial services internal governance requirements maintaining those logs as part of the documentation kept under that legislation (Article 26(6)).

rows.question: Is an AI that transcribes doctor-patient conversations prohibited? Or is it high-risk as per the use cases of Annex III of the AI Act?
rows.answer: An AI system that transcribes doctor, patient conversations is neither prohibited nor, in itself, a listed high-risk use case: it does not fall within any of the practices prohibited by Article 5, and Annex III's healthcare-related entries in point 5 cover evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services including healthcare, risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, and the evaluation and classification of emergency calls or dispatching and priority-setting of emergency first response services including emergency healthcare patient triage, not the documentation of a clinical consultation. It is high-risk only where it qualifies under the Annex I route in Article 6(1), that is where the transcription system is itself a product or a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (notably the medical devices legislation) and that product is subject to third-party conformity assessment. Where it neither meets that condition nor performs an Annex III function, it remains outside Chapter III, though Article 50 transparency obligations apply where the system is intended to interact directly with natural persons, requiring the provider to ensure the persons concerned are informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use. Classification must be assessed against the intended purpose declared by the provider, since a system that goes beyond transcription to generate clinical assessments may engage the Annex I route.

criteria.criterion: No, not a prohibited practice under Article 5
No, not high-risk under Annex III
Reason: narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), point (a)

rows.turn1_answer: An AI system that transcribes doctor, patient conversations is neither a prohibited practice nor an Annex III high-risk use case: it does not fall within any of the eight prohibited practices of Article 5, and Annex III contains no health-documentation entry, its point 5 healthcare-related items cover eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, and evaluation and classification of emergency calls and emergency healthcare patient triage, none of which describes speech-to-text documentation. Such a system would be high-risk only where it constitutes a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in notably the medical device and in vitro diagnostic device legislation, which is the Article 6(1) route; the Article 6(2) route via Annex III is not engaged. Where the transcription system is intended to interact directly with patients, the provider must, under Article 50(1), design it so that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use. Absent the Annex I safety component condition, the system falls outside the high-risk tier and is subject only to that transparency obligation.

rows.question: As a deployer, do I need to keep logs if I use a powerful LLM (surpassing the FLOPs threshold) for estimating whether customer payment confirmations are received via email?
rows.answer: No. Exceeding the compute threshold has no bearing on deployer duties: cumulative training compute above 10^25 floating point operations only triggers the presumption in Article 51(2) that a general-purpose AI model has high impact capabilities and is therefore classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, and the obligations flowing from that classification bind the provider of the model, not an entity using an AI system under its authority, which is a deployer within the meaning of Article 3(4). Record-keeping and the retention of automatically generated logs attach to high-risk AI systems, and estimating whether customer payment confirmations have been received by email is a narrow administrative task that does not fall within a high-risk use. The analysis changes only if the deployer becomes a provider under Article 25(1), that is by putting its name or trademark on the system, making a substantial modification to it, or modifying the intended purpose so that the system becomes high-risk, in which case the provider obligations, including record-keeping, would apply in full.

criteria.criterion: No
Article 26(6) logging duty applies only to deployers of high-risk AI systems
This use case is not a high-risk use case listed in Annex III
FLOPs threshold concerns GPAI systemic-risk classification under Article 51, a separate regime irrelevant to Annex III high-risk classification

rows.turn1_answer: No. The 10^25 FLOPs threshold in Article 51 merely triggers the presumption that a general-purpose AI model has high impact capabilities and is therefore a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, and the obligations flowing from that classification rest on the provider of the model, not on the deployer, which Article 3(4) defines as a person using an AI system under its authority outside a personal non-professional activity. Record-keeping and the retention of automatically generated logs attach to high-risk AI systems, and using a general-purpose AI system to estimate whether customer payment confirmations have arrived by email is an administrative back-office task that does not fall in a high-risk category. Model size alone never converts a deployer into a provider or creates a logging duty. That allocation shifts only if the deployer becomes a provider under Article 25 by putting its name or trademark on the system, making a substantial modification, or modifying the intended purpose so that the system becomes high-risk, in which case the provider obligations, including record-keeping, follow.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: AI software that assists clinicians in determining best treatment is high-risk under the Article 6(1) route where it constitutes a medical device, or a safety component of a product, covered by the medical devices legislation listed in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR) or Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (IVDR), and is required under that legislation to undergo third-party conformity assessment, which is typically the case for clinical decision support classified above Class I. Where that condition is met, the classification follows automatically from the product's regulatory status, and the Article 6(3) carve-outs for a narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns, or a preparatory task are unavailable, since those apply only to systems captured by Annex III. Annex III does not independently cover clinical treatment recommendations: its healthcare-related entries in point 5 concern evaluating eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services including healthcare services by or on behalf of public authorities, risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, and emergency healthcare patient triage systems and the dispatching of emergency first response services. The system is not among the practices exhaustively prohibited by Article 5, and where the Annex I condition is satisfied, the conformity assessment runs through the notified body route of the MDR or IVDR, resulting in a single CE marking, with the ISO 14971 and ISO 13485 processes serving as the practical basis for demonstrating compliance.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)

rows.turn1_answer: High-risk, and by the Annex I product safety route rather than the Annex III route. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk where it is itself a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Clinical decision support software that qualifies as a medical device falls under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices (or Regulation (EU) 2017/746 for in vitro diagnostic software), both listed in Annex I Section A, so the decisive condition is whether the device's risk class requires notified body conformity assessment, which is the case for everything above self-certified Class I. Annex III, which sets out the eight high-risk areas engaged through Article 6(2), is not the operative route, and the Article 6(3) derogation for a narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns, or a preparatory task applies only to Annex III systems and therefore cannot displace this classification.

rows.question: Do Annex I, Annex II, and Annex III all have to deal with high-risk AI classifications? If not, which doesn't/do not, and what is/are it/they about?
rows.answer: No, Annex II does not deal with high-risk classification, whereas Annex I and Annex III both do. Annex I lists the Union harmonisation legislation (Section A covering machinery, toys, radio equipment, medical devices, lifts and similar products, Section B covering civil aviation, motor vehicles, marine equipment, rail and agricultural vehicles), and under Article 6(1) an AI system that is itself such a product, or a safety component of one, is high-risk where that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment. Annex III sets out the eight high-risk areas whose listed lettered use cases make a system high-risk under Article 6(2), namely biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes, subject to the Article 6(3) derogation for systems posing no significant risk of harm that perform a narrow procedural task, improve a previously completed human activity, detect decision-making patterns without replacing the human assessment, or perform a preparatory task, unless the system performs profiling of natural persons. Annex II instead serves Article 5, listing the criminal offences for the narrow law-enforcement exception in Article 5(1)(h)(iii) to the prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces, being terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives, murder, grievous bodily injury, illicit trade in human organs or tissue, illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials, kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking, crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships, rape, environmental crime, organised or armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of those offences, each only where punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years.

criteria.criterion: No
Annex II is the one that does not - it lists criminal offences referred to in Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h)(iii), a prohibited-practices provision, not high-risk classification
Annex I and Annex III both relate to high-risk classification - Annex I (Union harmonisation legislation) feeds Article 6(1), Annex III (use-case areas) is referred to in Article 6(2)

rows.turn1_answer: No. Annex I and Annex III both feed high-risk classification: Annex I lists the Union harmonisation legislation covering products such as machinery, toys, lifts, medical devices, motor vehicles and rail, so that an AI system which is such a product or a safety component of one is high-risk under Article 6(1) where third-party conformity assessment is required, while Annex III sets out the eight areas whose listed use cases make a system high-risk under Article 6(2), namely biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Annex II has nothing to do with classification. It lists the criminal offences referred to in Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h)(iii), being terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives, murder, grievous bodily injury, illicit trade in human organs or tissue, illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials, kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking, crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships, rape, environmental crime, organised or armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of those offences. Its sole function is to delimit one of the narrow exceptions to the Article 5 prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, and it applies only where the offence is punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years.

rows.question: Is irregular migration a topic considered in the AI Act? If so, to what risk category does it belong?
rows.answer: Yes, irregular migration is expressly addressed, and AI systems concerning it are classified high-risk. Annex III, point 7(b) lists, within the area of migration, asylum and border control management and in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law, AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assess a risk, including a security risk, a risk of irregular migration, or a health risk, posed by a natural person who intends to enter or who has entered into the territory of a Member State; such systems are high-risk by virtue of Article 6(2). The derogation in Article 6(3) can remove such a system from the high-risk tier where it merely performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, but never where the system performs profiling of natural persons, which a risk assessment of an individual traveller will typically involve. Because the deployers are bodies governed by public law or entities acting on their behalf, Article 27 additionally requires a fundamental rights impact assessment prior to first use, covering the deployment processes, duration and frequency of use, affected categories of persons, specific risks of harm, human oversight measures and mitigation arrangements.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III.7)
High-risk

rows.turn1_answer: Yes, irregular migration is expressly addressed, and AI systems assessing it are high-risk. Annex III, point 7(b) lists, within the area of migration, asylum and border control management and in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law, AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assess a risk, including a security risk, a risk of irregular migration, or a health risk, posed by a natural person who intends to enter or who has entered into the territory of a Member State; Article 6(2) makes any system referred to in Annex III high-risk. The derogation in Article 6(3) can displace that classification only where the system performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, and it never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, which a risk assessment of this kind will typically involve.

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes to the date of release, yes to the number of parameters, yes to the model's interaction with hardware, yes to the licence, and no to samples of outlier data used in training. Article 53(1)(b) requires the provider of a general-purpose AI model to draw up, keep up to date and make available to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate the model information that gives them a good understanding of the model's capabilities and limitations and that contains, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex XII, which expressly list the date of release and methods of distribution, how the model interacts or can be used to interact with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself where applicable, the architecture and number of parameters, and the licence for the model, alongside the intended tasks and types of AI systems for integration, the acceptable use policies, the versions of relevant software where applicable, and the modality and format of inputs and outputs. Annex XII calls for a summary of the content used for training rather than any disclosure of data samples, so outlier examples need not be supplied to downstream providers, and this documentation duty operates without prejudice to intellectual property rights and confidential business information or trade secrets. Under the Article 53(2) carve-out the Annex XII downstream-provider information duty falls away for models released under a free and open-source licence permitting access, use, modification and distribution with publicly available parameters, unless the model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51.

criteria.criterion: Date of release - Yes
Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No

rows.turn1_answer: Yes to the first four, no to the fifth. The information and documentation supplied under Article 53(1)(b) to providers of AI systems intending to integrate the model must contain at a minimum the elements of Annex XII, which expressly include the date of release and methods of distribution, the architecture and number of parameters, how the model interacts or can be used to interact with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself where applicable, and the licence for the model, alongside the intended tasks and integration types, acceptable use policies, relevant software versions where applicable, and the modality and format of inputs and outputs. Samples of outlier data are not required: Annex XII calls only for a general description of the training, testing and validation data, including type and provenance and curation methodologies, and Article 53(1)(d) separately requires a publicly available sufficiently detailed summary of the training content, with no obligation to disclose data samples, all without prejudice to intellectual property rights and confidential business information or trade secrets. Note that under Article 53(2) the Annex XII downstream information duty does not apply to a model released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, architecture and usage information, unless the model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51.

rows.question: Who, if at all, needs to establish the post-market monitoring system for a high-risk AI system? Provider/deployer/AI office? Is it possible that the monitoring system may need to also include info on interaction with other AI systems than the high-risk one in consideration?
rows.answer: The provider bears this duty: Article 72(1) requires providers to establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system, and Article 17 requires that its setting-up, implementation and maintenance be embedded in the provider's quality management system. Deployers and the AI Office do not establish it, although Article 72(2) contemplates that the relevant data on performance throughout the system's lifetime may be provided by deployers or collected through other sources, and a deployer that puts its name or trademark on the system, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose is itself considered a provider under Article 25(1) and assumes the obligation. Yes, Article 72(2) states that, where relevant, post-market monitoring shall include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems, so monitoring can extend beyond the high-risk AI system in question. That same provision carves out sensitive operational data of deployers which are law-enforcement authorities, and the data gathered feeds back into the risk management system under Article 9, which requires evaluation of other risks arising from post-market monitoring data.

criteria.criterion: Provider
Not deployer or AI Office
Yes — must include analysis of interaction with other AI systems where relevant

rows.turn1_answer: The provider, not the deployer and not the AI Office, must establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system under Article 72(1), and Article 17(1) requires that the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of that system be embedded in the provider's quality management system. Under Article 72(2) the system must actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data on performance throughout the system's lifetime, whether provided by deployers or collected through other sources, so the provider can evaluate continuous compliance with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, and that data must feed the evaluation of further risks in the risk management system under Article 9. Yes: where relevant, post-market monitoring shall include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems, subject to the express carve-out that the obligation does not cover sensitive operational data of deployers which are law-enforcement authorities. A deployer or other third party that puts its name or trademark on the system, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose becomes a provider under Article 25(1) and then assumes this monitoring duty itself.

rows.question: What is an "area" and what is a "use case" for high-risk as per Article 6(2)? How many areas exist?
rows.answer: Under Article 6(2), which provides that AI systems referred to in Annex III are high-risk, an "area" is one of the numbered headings of Annex III, and a "use case" is a lettered entry set out beneath that heading, so that only a system falling within a listed lettered use case is caught, subject to the Article 6(3) derogation for systems posing no significant risk of harm because they perform a narrow procedural task, improve the result of a previously completed human activity, detect decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment, or perform a preparatory task, unless the system performs profiling of natural persons. Eight areas exist. They are biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment, workers' management and access to self-employment, access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes.

criteria.criterion: Area = broad Annex III numbered heading/policy domain
Use case = specific application listed within an area (lettered sub-point)
8 areas exist

rows.turn1_answer: Under Article 6(2), an AI system is high-risk where it falls within one of the use cases listed in Annex III: an "area" is a numbered heading of Annex III describing a field of deployment, while a "use case" is a lettered entry under that heading describing the specific intended purpose that triggers the classification, so listing in an area alone is insufficient and the system must match a listed use case. Annex III sets out eight areas: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. This structure also frames the delegated-act power in Article 7(1), under which the Commission may add or modify use cases only within the areas already listed in Annex III and only where the risk is equivalent to or greater than that of the systems already listed.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: Not as a standalone area, though several healthcare uses are captured. Annex III lists eight high-risk areas: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes, and only a lettered use case within one of those areas makes a system high-risk under Article 6(2). Clinical decision making is not itself listed, but Annex III point 5 covers evaluation by or on behalf of public authorities of eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services including healthcare services, risk assessment and pricing in relation to life and health insurance, and the evaluation and classification of emergency calls and dispatch priority for emergency first response services including medical aid and emergency healthcare patient triage systems. Independently, Article 6(1) makes an AI system high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I, which includes the medical devices and in vitro diagnostic medical devices regulations, provided that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment, so most AI-driven diagnostic or therapeutic devices are high-risk by that route rather than through Annex III.

criteria.criterion: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No

rows.turn1_answer: Annex III sets out eight high-risk areas: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Healthcare decision making is not itself one of those areas, and under Article 6(2) only a use case actually listed under one of those headings is high-risk by that route. Health-related use cases do appear under Annex III point 5 on essential services, namely evaluation by or on behalf of public authorities of natural persons' eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services including healthcare services, risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, and evaluation and classification of emergency calls or the dispatching and prioritisation of emergency first response services including medical aid, as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems.
