Separately, the Annex I route in Article 6(1) classifies as high-risk an AI system that is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the listed Union harmonisation legislation, which includes medical devices and in vitro diagnostic medical devices, where that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation.

rows.question: What does Annex VII point 5.1 say? Try to get the substance right. Do not get confused with other material, like 5.1 in Annex III or Article 7, which is about something else entirely.
rows.answer: Annex VII point 5.1 is the opening provision of the section on surveillance of the approved quality management system, and it states that the purpose of the surveillance carried out by the notified body is to make sure that the provider duly and properly fulfils the terms and conditions of the approved quality management system. It is therefore an ongoing supervision rule directed at the notified body, sitting after point 4 on control of the technical documentation, under which the notified body examines the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV and, where the system conforms to the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2, issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Annex VII as a whole is the conformity assessment procedure based on assessment of the quality management system put in place under Article 17 plus assessment of the technical documentation, with notified body involvement, and it applies to Annex III point 1 biometric systems where harmonised standards or common specifications have not been fully applied. It has no connection to Article 7, which empowers the Commission to amend Annex III by delegated act, nor to Annex III point 5 on essential private and public services.

criteria.criterion: Purpose of surveillance is to ensure the provider duly complies with the terms and conditions of the approved quality management system

rows.turn1_answer: Annex VII point 5.1 opens point 5 of that Annex, on surveillance of the approved quality management system: it provides that the purpose of the surveillance carried out by the notified body is to ensure that the provider duly fulfils the terms and conditions of the approved quality management system. It therefore sits after point 4 of Annex VII, which governs control of the technical documentation and culminates in the notified body's issuance (or refusal) of a Union technical documentation assessment certificate, and it establishes the ongoing supervisory phase rather than the initial assessment. Annex VII as a whole is the conformity assessment procedure based on assessment of the quality management system and assessment of the technical documentation, with notified body involvement.

rows.question: Do providers of GPAI systems, even if not with systemic risk, have an obligation to extensively shield their models from adversarial attacks? What about specifically for adversarial images? What about specifically for prompt injection?
rows.answer: Systemic risk applies to general-purpose AI models, not to AI systems. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.

criteria.criterion: No
Applies only to GPAI models with systemic risk, under Article 55(1)(a)
Adversarial images not separately addressed - only general adversarial-testing duty
Prompt injection not separately addressed - not mentioned in Article 55

rows.turn1_answer: Systemic risk applies to general-purpose AI models, not to AI systems. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a model with systemic risk where it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating point operations. The Commission may also designate a model on the basis of the Annex XIII criteria. A model classified as having systemic risk then carries the additional Article 55 obligations: model evaluation including adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, serious-incident reporting, and adequate cybersecurity. The high-risk regime for AI systems under Articles 6 and Annex III is a separate classification and does not use the systemic-risk concept.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No, introducing guardrails does not move a system out of the high-risk tier. Classification under Article 6 is fixed by the system itself and its intended purpose, namely whether it is, or is a safety component of, a product covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation subject to third-party conformity assessment, or whether it falls within one of the Annex III use-cases, and guardrails operate instead as the targeted mitigation and risk-control measures required by the risk management system under Article 9 (and as limitations and known risks to be stated in the instructions for use under Article 13). Changing the capabilities and intended purpose can change the classification, because Article 6(2) turns on the intended purpose falling within an Annex III use-case, and Article 6(3) takes an Annex III system out of high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and does no more than perform a narrow procedural task, improve the result of a previously completed human activity, detect decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or perform a preparatory task, unless it profiles natural persons, with the provider documenting that self-assessment before placing the system on the market. The reverse move is expressly regulated: under Article 25(1) a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party that makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose so that the system becomes high-risk, itself becomes a provider bearing the Article 16 provider obligations, and only the Commission may delete a use-case from Annex III by delegated act under Article 7(3), where the system no longer poses significant risks and the deletion does not lower the overall level of protection.

criteria.criterion: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes

rows.turn1_answer: No, guardrails cannot move a system out of the high-risk tier, and the Regulation recognises no "moderate risk" tier in any event. Classification under Article 6 turns on objective features of the system rather than on the mitigations wrapped around it, namely whether it is a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I that must undergo third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)), or whether its intended purpose falls within a lettered use case under one of the eight Annex III areas (Article 6(2)), so guardrails are a consequence of high-risk status rather than a route out of it. Changing the capabilities and the intended purpose can change the classification: a system whose intended purpose no longer corresponds to any Annex III use case is not high-risk by that route, and Article 6(3) removes an Annex III system from high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and is intended to perform a narrow procedural task, to improve the result of a previously completed human activity, to detect decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment, or to perform a preparatory task, with the derogation never available where the system performs profiling of natural persons, and the provider must document that assessment before the system is placed on the market. Where such a change is made to a system already assessed, Article 43(4) requires a new conformity assessment in the event of a substantial modification, and Article 25 makes any actor that modifies the intended purpose so that the system becomes high-risk a provider bearing the full provider obligations.

rows.question: Can law enforcement starts using a real-time remote biometric identification system without prior authorisation? If yes, how much time do they have to seek authorisation, and what happens if the authorisation is refused?
rows.answer: Yes, but only exceptionally and subject to a strict after-the-fact authorisation duty. The use of "real-time" remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement is a prohibited practice under Article 5(1)(h) unless strictly necessary for one of three exhaustively listed objectives, namely the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation and the search for missing persons, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack, and the localisation or identification of a person suspected of an offence referred to in Annex II punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years, with each such use requiring prior judicial or administrative authorisation and Member States free under Article 5(5) to enable these exceptions in national law or to impose stricter rules. Where there is a duly justified situation of urgency for exceptional reasons of public security or a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, Article 46(2) allows law-enforcement authorities to put the system into service before authorisation, provided that the authorisation is requested during or after the use without undue delay. If the authorisation is refused, the use must be stopped with immediate effect and all results and outputs of that use must be immediately discarded.

criteria.criterion: Yes, but only in a duly justified situation of urgency
Authorisation must be requested without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours
If refused: use stopped immediately, all data/results/outputs discarded and deleted

rows.turn1_answer: Yes, but only in a duly justified situation of urgency. Article 5 prohibits the use of "real-time" remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement unless and in so far as strictly necessary for one of three exhaustively listed objectives, namely the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings and the search for missing persons, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack, and the localisation or identification of a person suspected of a criminal offence referred to in Annex II punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order of a maximum period of at least four years, each such deployment requiring authorisation by a judicial or independent administrative authority before use. In a duly justified situation of urgency under Article 5 the use may be commenced without that prior authorisation, provided the authorisation is requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours, and if the authorisation is refused the use must be stopped with immediate effect and all data, results and outputs discarded and deleted. A parallel rule applies to the separate derogation from conformity assessment in Article 46, under which law-enforcement authorities may in urgency put a specific high-risk AI system into service without the market surveillance authority's authorisation provided it is requested during or after use without undue delay, and refusal again requires the use to stop with immediate effect and all results and outputs to be immediately discarded.

rows.question: Consider a private contractor of the municipality that runs a city's emergency-call triage platform. The contractor plans to use an AI tool to prioritize police response decisions. Before going live with the system, does this contractor need to look into fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA)? Is this because of this scenario belonging to Annex III 5(b) or 5(c)? What about private contractors offering other public services concerning Annex III but NOT specifically 5(b) or 5(c)?
rows.answer: Yes, a fundamental rights impact assessment is required before first use, but not on the 5(b) or 5(c) ground. The emergency-call triage and police dispatch prioritisation use case falls under Annex III point 5(d), covering AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons or to dispatch, or establish priority in the dispatching of, emergency first response services including by police, firefighters and medical aid; the FRIA duty arises instead because Article 27(1) binds deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, which is the contractor's status here, and the separately listed points 5(b) creditworthiness and credit scoring and 5(c) life and health insurance risk assessment and pricing exist only to catch deployers that are neither public bodies nor public-service providers. The same logic extends across Annex III: a private contractor providing public services must perform the assessment for any high-risk system it deploys, whatever the Annex III area, with the single exception in Article 27(1) of systems intended for the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, critical infrastructure. The assessment must describe the deployment processes, the period and frequency of intended use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to them, the implementation of human oversight measures, and the measures on materialisation of those risks including internal governance and complaint mechanisms, and its results must be notified to the market surveillance authority.

criteria.criterion: Yes, FRIA required
No — trigger is being a "private entity providing public services" under Article 27(1), not Annex III 5(b)/(c)
5(b)/(c) is a separate, additional limb pulling in deployers of those specific systems even when not providing public services
Other private contractors offering public services outside 5(b)/(c) remain covered via the general public-service limb, for every Annex III area except point 2

rows.turn1_answer: Yes, the contractor must perform the fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, but not on the basis of points 5(b) or 5(c) of Annex III. Article 27(1) imposes the assessment on deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, for any high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), and separately on deployers of the point 5(b) creditworthiness and credit scoring systems and the point 5(c) life and health insurance risk assessment and pricing systems; the contractor qualifies under the first limb as a private entity providing a public service, its system falling under Annex III point 5(d) covering AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls or to establish priority in the dispatching of emergency first response services, including by police. The assessment must describe the deployer's processes in line with the intended purpose, the period and frequency of intended use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to them in light of the provider's Article 13 information on transparency and interpretability of outputs, the implementation of human oversight measures per the instructions for use, and the measures on materialisation of those risks including internal governance and complaint mechanisms, with notification of the results to the market surveillance authority under Article 27(3). Private contractors providing public services are likewise caught for high-risk systems in any other Annex III area, since the point 5(b) and 5(c) limb only extends the duty to deployers who are neither public bodies nor public service providers; the sole exception is the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, critical infrastructure, which Article 27(1) carves out entirely.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

criteria.criterion: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here

rows.turn1_answer: No. Under Article 50(4), the deployer's duty to disclose that image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake has been artificially generated or manipulated does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences. Absent that law-enforcement authorisation, the deployer must disclose that the content is a deep fake.

rows.question: If a high-risk AI system was already placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026, does the AI Act fully apply to it? What about general purpose AI systems?
rows.answer: No, not fully. Under the transitional provisions in Article 111, a high-risk AI system placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 is caught by the Regulation only if, as from that date, it is subject to significant changes in its design, subject to two qualifications: the prohibited practices in Article 5 apply irrespective of that grandfathering, and providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities must in any case take the necessary steps to comply by 2 August 2030. General-purpose AI models are treated separately: models placed on the market before 2 August 2025, the date from which the Chapter V obligations became applicable under Article 113, must be brought into compliance by 2 August 2027, which covers the Article 53 provider duties (technical documentation per Annex XI, information and documentation for downstream providers of AI systems per Annex XII, a policy to comply with Union copyright law, and a publicly available sufficiently detailed summary of the training content) and, for a model classified as having systemic risk under Article 51, the additional Article 55 duties of model evaluation including adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Where the AI system is a component of a large-scale IT system established by an act listed in Annex X and was placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027, compliance is required only by 31 December 2030.

criteria.criterion: No, does not fully apply
Applies only if system undergoes significant changes in design as from 2 August 2026
High-risk systems for public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030 regardless
GPAI models placed on market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027

rows.turn1_answer: No, not fully. Under the transitional provisions of Article 111, high-risk AI systems placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026 fall under the Regulation only if, as from that date, they are subject to significant changes in their designs, save that providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities must comply in any event by 2 August 2030, and the prohibited practices in Article 5 apply from 2 February 2025 irrespective of that grandfathering. For general-purpose AI models, the Chapter V obligations apply from 2 August 2025 under Article 113, but providers of models placed on the market before that date have until 2 August 2027 to take the necessary steps to comply, which for the Article 53 duties means the technical documentation per Annex XI, the information and documentation for downstream providers per Annex XII, the copyright policy, and the publicly available sufficiently detailed summary of training content. Where the model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51, the additional Article 55 duties of model evaluation including adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and cybersecurity protection of the model and its physical infrastructure are subject to the same 2 August 2027 deadline for pre-existing models.

rows.question: What is Annex X about? What is it used for?
rows.answer: Annex X imposes no obligations of its own. It is a list of Union legislative acts on large-scale IT systems in the area of Freedom, Security and Justice, naming seven: the Schengen Information System, the Visa Information System, Eurodac, the Entry/Exit System, the European Travel Information and Authorisation System, the European Criminal Records Information System on third-country nationals and stateless persons, and the two interoperability Regulations. Its operative function is to fix a transitional timeline under Article 111(1), which provides that AI systems that are components of the large-scale IT systems established by the acts listed in Annex X and placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027 must be brought into compliance with the Regulation only by 31 December 2030, without prejudice to the prohibited practices in Article 5. Article 111(1) also requires the Regulation's requirements to be taken into account in the evaluation of each of those large-scale IT systems provided for in those acts, and where those acts are replaced or amended.

criteria.criterion: Annex X lists Union legislative acts on large-scale IT systems in the area of Freedom, Security and Justice (e.g. SIS, VIS, Eurodac, EES, ETIAS, ECRIS-TCN, interoperability regulations)
Used in conjunction with Article 111 to set transitional/compliance deadlines for AI systems that are components of these large-scale IT systems

rows.turn1_answer: Annex X is not the annex containing the EU declaration of conformity; it is a list of Union legislative acts on large-scale IT systems in the area of Freedom, Security and Justice, imposing no obligations of its own and naming seven systems: the Schengen Information System, the Visa Information System, Eurodac, the Entry/Exit System, the European Travel Information and Authorisation System, the European Criminal Records Information System on third-country nationals and stateless persons, and the two interoperability Regulations. Its sole function is to fix the transitional timeline in Article 47's neighbouring transitional rule, Article 111, under which AI systems that are components of those large-scale IT systems and were placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027 need only be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030. The EU declaration of conformity is instead governed by Article 47, which requires the provider to draw up a written, machine readable, physically or electronically signed declaration for each high-risk AI system stating that it meets the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, to keep it up to date and at the disposal of the national competent authorities for 10 years, to translate it into a language easily understood by those authorities, and to merge it into a single declaration where other Union harmonisation legislation also requires one. Its content is set out in Annex V: the AI system name, type and unambiguous reference, the provider's or authorised representative's name and address, a statement that the declaration is issued under the provider's sole responsibility, a statement of conformity with this Regulation and any other relevant Union law, references to harmonised standards or common specifications applied, where applicable the notified body's name and identification number with the conformity assessment procedure and certificate, and the place and date of issue with the signatory's name, function and signature.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: Not high-risk, and not a prohibited practice. The Article 5(1)(c) social scoring prohibition is not engaged because the tool does not evaluate or classify natural persons over a certain period of time on the basis of their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics to produce a social score, and any resulting bag check arises in the same transactional context in which the data was generated and is proportionate to the observed conduct, so neither subpoint (i) nor (ii) is satisfied. Article 5(1)(d) is likewise not engaged: the system does not assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics, and the express carve-out in that point covers AI systems used to support the human assessment of involvement in a criminal activity that is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to that activity, which is what current-cart and checkout anomalies, verified by an optional manual staff check, amount to. Retail loss prevention of this kind corresponds to no lettered use-case in the Annex III areas, so the resemblance the retailer draws to law enforcement does not carry it into the high-risk tier; it would become high-risk only if the tool were reconfigured into an Annex III use-case, for example by processing biometric data for remote biometric identification or biometric categorisation.

criteria.criterion: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions

rows.turn1_answer: Not prohibited and not high-risk, on the facts described. Article 5(1)(c) social scoring does not apply because the tool does not evaluate or classify natural persons over a certain period of time on the basis of their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, and produces no social score leading to detrimental or unfavourable treatment in unrelated social contexts or treatment unjustified or disproportionate to the gravity of the behaviour; a single-transaction anomaly flag in the same context in which the data was generated falls outside that prohibition, which binds private deployers as much as public ones. Article 5(1)(d) is likewise not engaged: the tool does not make risk assessments predicting the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics, and it instead supports the human assessment of involvement in a possible criminal activity on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to that activity, cart contents and checkout discrepancies, which the express carve-out in Article 5(1)(d) excludes from the prohibition. High-risk classification under Article 6(2) arises only where a system falls within a listed use-case of Annex III, and the law enforcement use-cases there concern use by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, not a retailer's own loss-prevention checks, while the absence of biometrics keeps it outside the biometrics area; the retailer's "high risk like policing" characterisation is therefore not supported, leaving the system subject only to the AI literacy duty under Article 4.

rows.question: We are a private educational institution intending to deploy an AI tool that analyses students' prior grades and learning outcomes to recommend whether they should follow the standard or accelerated honours track going forward. We remark that a student who receives the "standard" recommendation is *not* barred from choosing accelerated, the system merely provides a suggestion. Are there reasons to believe the system might be high-risk? What articles/annex and specific points, if any, concern this use case?
rows.answer: Likely high-risk, and the advisory-only character of the recommendation does not change that: the tool is an AI system intended to be used to evaluate learning outcomes, including when those outcomes are used to steer the learning process of natural persons in educational and vocational training institutions at all levels (Annex III, point 3(b)), and to assess the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or will be able to access (Annex III, point 3(c)), which brings it within the Annex III route to high-risk classification under Article 6(2). The Article 6(3) derogation, for systems performing a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment absent proper human review, or performing a preparatory task, is unlikely to be available, because the recommendation is designed to influence the track a student takes rather than merely prepare or refine a human assessment, and in any event an Annex III system shall always be considered high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons, which an individualised evaluation of a student's grade history will normally constitute. Nothing described engages the prohibited tier: Article 5 would bite only if the tool were used to infer emotions of natural persons in the area of education institutions outside medical or safety reasons, or deployed subliminal, purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques materially distorting students' behaviour so as to cause significant harm. As deployer, the institution should therefore treat the system as high-risk and satisfy itself that it bears CE marking and is accompanied by the provider's instructions for use before putting it into service.

criteria.criterion: Yes
Annex III point 3(c) - assessing appropriate level of education a person will receive/access
Article 6(3) derogation for narrow/preparatory/non-influencing tasks would otherwise apply given the non-binding recommendation
Article 6(3) final subparagraph - Annex III systems are always high-risk if they profile natural persons, overriding the derogation

rows.turn1_answer: Likely high-risk, and the advisory-only character does not change that. The system falls under Article 6(2) via Annex III, point 3, which designates education and vocational training uses as a high-risk area, specifically point 3(b), AI systems intended to be used to evaluate learning outcomes, including when those outcomes are used to steer the learning process, and point 3(c), AI systems used to assess the appropriate level of education an individual will receive or will be able to access, both of which describe a tool that reads prior grades and learning outcomes to route a student towards a standard or accelerated honours track. The Article 6(3) derogation, for systems performing a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performing a preparatory task, is unlikely to rescue it, because a track recommendation materially influences the outcome of decision making rather than merely preparing it, and in any event that derogation never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, which an individualised assessment built on a student's own attainment record ordinarily does. Accordingly the institution should treat itself as deployer of a high-risk AI system in the area listed in point 3 of Annex III.

rows.question: We manufactured an industrial robot with an embedded AI module that decides when to reduce speed near human workers to prevent hurting them. The robot is covered by the Machinery Regulation, listed in Annex I of the AI Act. We already underwent conformity assessment with a notified body and got a CE mark for the robot. Do we need the AI module undergo a separate AI Act conformity assessment dedicated to the AI Act? Do we need to submit the system to the EU database of high-risk AI systems?
rows.answer: No separate, standalone AI Act conformity assessment is required. Under Article 43(3), for high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, the provider follows the relevant conformity assessment procedure required under that sectoral act, and the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements apply to the AI module and form part of that single assessment, with the notified body notified under the Machinery Regulation entitled to control conformity with those requirements. Points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply to that assessment, giving the notified body access to the training, validation and testing data sets, the power to require further evidence or tests, access where strictly necessary to the training and trained models, and the duty to state reasons where it refuses certification, so if the completed machinery assessment did not in fact examine the Section 2 requirements it must be extended to cover them, and Article 43(4) requires a new conformity assessment upon any substantial modification, excluding changes pre-determined by the provider at the initial assessment. As to registration, no: the EU database maintained by the Commission under Article 71 holds high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2), registered by the provider under Article 49 before placing on the market, whereas a safety component of an Annex I product is high-risk under Article 6(1) and therefore falls outside that registration obligation.

criteria.criterion: No
AI Act Section 2 requirements incorporated into existing Machinery Regulation conformity assessment, not a separate AI Act procedure (Article 43(3))
No EU database registration, since Article 71 applies only to Annex III high-risk systems, not Article 6(1)/Annex I product-related ones

rows.turn1_answer: No separate AI Act conformity assessment is required, because Article 43(3) provides that for high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I the provider follows the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedure, and the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 apply to the system and shall be part of that single assessment. That means the existing machinery procedure must be extended to cover the AI Act requirements rather than repeated: points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply, so the notified body must be granted access to the training, validation and testing data sets, may require further evidence or tests, and may in the last resort obtain access to the training and trained models, and the notified body notified under the machinery legislation may control conformity with Section 2 only where its compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) has been assessed in its notification. Registration in the EU database is not required here, since the database established under Article 71 covers high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2), that is Annex III use-case systems, together with systems registered under Articles 49 and 60 and systems assessed as not high-risk under Article 6(3), and not safety components of Annex I products classified high-risk under Article 6(1). Under Article 43(4), a new conformity assessment becomes necessary in the event of a substantial modification of the AI module, although changes to performance pre-determined by the provider at the initial assessment and documented in the technical documentation do not count as such.Note also that, under Article 113, the obligations for high-risk AI systems that are safety components of products covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation apply from 2 August 2027, so the AI Act requirements must be integrated into the operator's machinery conformity assessment by that date.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No. Under Article 43(3), which governs conformity assessment of high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 apply to those systems and form part of the sectoral assessment. Where the sectoral act permits the product manufacturer to opt out of a third-party conformity assessment on the basis that it has applied all harmonised standards covering the relevant sectoral requirements, that option may be used only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards published under Article 40 or, where applicable, common specifications adopted by the Commission under Article 41 covering all requirements set out in Section 2. Dispensing with notified body involvement therefore removes only the third-party control, not the substantive Section 2 requirements, and compliance with the sectoral standards alone does not discharge them.

criteria.criterion: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones

rows.turn1_answer: No. Article 43(3), which integrates the AI Act assessment into the sectoral procedure for high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, states that the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 apply to those systems and form part of that assessment. Where the sectoral act allows the product manufacturer to opt out of a third-party conformity assessment on the basis that it has applied all harmonised standards covering the relevant requirements, that option may be used only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications under Article 41 covering all requirements set out in Section 2. The opt-out therefore presupposes full compliance with Section 2 and confirms it rather than displacing it, so the absence of a notified body changes only how conformity is demonstrated, not which substantive requirements must be met.

rows.question: A private contractor runs a region's gas supply service on behalf of the local government. It licenses an AI system from a vendor, fine-tunes it on local data, and then puts it into service under its own brand. To learn about correct applicable classifications of the system and the contractor, what material of the AI Act should I read? Does fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) applies?
rows.answer: No, a fundamental rights impact assessment is not required here. Article 27(1) obliges deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services to assess the impact on fundamental rights before deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), but it expressly excepts systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, which is critical infrastructure covering the supply of gas, so the exception applies to this contractor even though it is a private entity providing a public service. For the classifications themselves, the material to read is Article 6(2) together with point 2 of Annex III, which classifies AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of the supply of gas as high-risk, and Article 25(1), under which a deployer or other third party that puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (point (a)) or makes a substantial modification to it (point (b)) is considered the provider and assumes the provider obligations under Article 16. Article 25(2) then removes the licensing vendor from the role of provider for that specific system and requires it to cooperate closely with the new provider and make available the necessary information and reasonably expected technical access, unless it had clearly specified that its system was not to be turned into a high-risk AI system. To the extent the contractor also uses the system, Article 26 continues to apply, requiring use in accordance with the instructions for use, human oversight by competent and trained natural persons, monitoring with notification of the market surveillance authority and suspension where a risk arises, and retention of automatically generated logs for at least six months.

rows.turn1_answer: No, no fundamental rights impact assessment is required here. Article 27 obliges deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services to assess the impact on fundamental rights before deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), but it expressly excepts high-risk AI systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, which is the critical infrastructure area covering the supply of gas, so the exception removes this deployment from the Article 27 duty. On the actor classification, the material to read is Article 25(1) on responsibilities along the AI value chain: a deployer that puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market, or that makes a substantial modification to it so that it remains high-risk, is considered the provider and assumes the provider obligations under Article 16, while Article 25(2) provides that the initial provider ceases to be the provider of that specific system and must cooperate closely and make available the necessary information and reasonably expected technical access. On the system classification, Article 6(2) read together with point 2 of Annex III is the operative material for determining high-risk status as a safety component in the management and operation of critical infrastructure, and to the extent the contractor also uses the system it remains bound by the deployer duties in Article 26, including use in accordance with the instructions for use, assignment of human oversight to competent and trained natural persons, monitoring of operation, and retention of automatically generated logs for at least six months.
